stem: A partially condensed structure is CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. What is its molecular formula?
why: Count the carbons (3), the hydrogens (3 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 8) and the oxygen (1).

stem: Which statement about molecular formulas is correct?
why: The molecular formula gives only the number of each kind of atom. Constitutional isomers share a formula.

o.v: A molecular formula shows which atoms are bonded to each other
Every molecular formula corresponds to exactly one compound
A molecular formula does not show how the atoms are connected, so C₄H₁₀O fits several different compounds
A molecular formula shows the lone pairs on each atom

stem: Which bond-line structure is the same compound as the condensed structure (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃?
why: (CH₃)₂CH- is a carbon with two methyl groups; attached to CH₂CH₃ it gives 2-methylbutane.

stem: Write the molecular formula for CH₃CH₂COCH₃.
why: Four carbons, 3 + 2 + 0 + 3 = 8 hydrogens, one oxygen.

stem: Draw the complete Lewis structure of CH₃OCH₃ (dimethyl ether), showing every lone pair. How many lone pairs are there in total?
why: Each carbon has four bonds and no lone pairs. Oxygen forms two bonds and keeps two lone pairs.
a: Two lone pairs, both on the oxygen atom.

stem: Give two different compounds with the molecular formula C₂H₆O as condensed structures.
why: They are constitutional isomers: the same formula with different connectivity.

stem: The bond-line structure of 2-methylbutane is shown. Write its partially condensed structure and its molecular formula.
why: Each vertex and line end is a carbon. The branch point carbon bears one hydrogen; the CH₂ has two and each CH₃ has three: 3 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 12.

stem: How many carbon atoms are in the compound shown?
why: Count each vertex and line end: the chain has 6 carbons plus one methyl branch.

stem: What is the molecular formula of the compound shown?
why: Five carbons; the CH₃, CH₃, CH, CH₂ carbons carry 3 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 9 hydrogens, plus the acid O-H = 10.

stem: Which statement about bond-line structures is correct?
why: Bond-line structures omit carbon labels and C-H hydrogens; each carbon is assumed to have enough hydrogens for four bonds.

o.v: Carbon atoms are at each bend and line end, and hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon are not drawn
Every hydrogen atom must be drawn
Carbon atoms are written as the letter C
Lone pairs on oxygen must always be drawn

stem: How many hydrogen atoms are bonded to the carbon that bears the OH group?
why: That carbon has bonds to OH, CH₃ and CH₂ (three bonds), so one hydrogen completes four bonds.

stem: Which compound has the molecular formula C₆H₁₂O?
why: Only 4-methyl-2-pentanone gives six carbons and twelve hydrogens with one oxygen (the others are C₇H₁₄O, C₆H₁₄O and C₆H₁₀O₂).

stem: Draw the bond-line structure of (CH₃)₂CHCH₂CH₃.
why: Each vertex is a carbon; the CH branch carries one methyl group.
a: The bond-line structure is a four-carbon chain with a methyl branch on the second carbon (2-methylbutane).

stem: Draw the bond-line structure of CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃.
why: Draw the zigzag chain and attach OH to the second carbon.
a: A four-carbon chain with an OH group on carbon 2 (2-butanol).

stem: What is the molecular formula of the compound shown?
why: Seven carbons; hydrogens: 3 + 3 + 3 + 0 + 2 + 3 = 14 (the quaternary carbon has none); one oxygen.

stem: Draw bond-line structures of all constitutional isomers of C₄H₁₀.
why: Only these two carbon skeletons are possible with four carbons.
a: Two isomers: butane (an unbranched chain) and 2-methylpropane (isobutane).

stem: For the compound shown, give the molecular formula and identify the carbon atom that bears no hydrogen atoms.
why: Carbon atoms: CH₃ (3), CH₂ (2), C=O (0), O-CH₂ (2), CH₃ (3): ten hydrogens in total.
a: C₅H₁₀O₂; the carbonyl (C=O) carbon has no hydrogens.

stem: Which functional group is present in this compound?
why: The OH group on a carbon atom is an alcohol.

stem: Which functional group is present in this compound?
why: A carbonyl group bonded to two carbons is a ketone.

stem: Which functional group is present in this compound?
why: C(=O)-O-C: a carbonyl carbon bonded to an OR group.

stem: Which functional group is present in this compound?
why: The C≡N group is a nitrile.

stem: Which functional group is present in this compound?
why: A carbonyl group bonded directly to nitrogen is an amide.

stem: Which pair of functional groups (besides the aromatic ring) is present in aspirin?
why: The acetyl group is attached through oxygen (an ester), and the other substituent is CO₂H.

o.v: An ester and a carboxylic acid
A ketone and a carboxylic acid
An ether and a carboxylic acid

stem: Name the functional group in CH₃CH₂CHO.
why: A carbonyl group with at least one hydrogen attached to the carbonyl carbon.

stem: Identify the functional group and classify it as primary, secondary or tertiary.
why: Count the carbon atoms bonded to nitrogen: one.
a: An amine; it is primary because nitrogen is bonded to one carbon.

stem: Identify the two functional groups in this compound.
why: The C=C is an alkene; the OH on an sp³ carbon is an alcohol.

stem: Identify the two carbonyl-containing functional groups in this compound.
why: CO₂H is a carboxylic acid; C(=O)N is an amide.
a: A carboxylic acid and an amide.

stem: Draw one aldehyde and one ketone, each with the molecular formula C₃H₆O.
why: Both are constitutional isomers with the carbonyl group in different positions.
a: Propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO) is the aldehyde and acetone (CH₃COCH₃) is the ketone.

stem: Is the compound shown an amine or an amide? Explain.
why: An amine has nitrogen bonded only to carbon and hydrogen atoms that are not part of a carbonyl group.
a: It is an amide, because nitrogen is bonded directly to the carbonyl carbon.

stem: A carbon atom with a positive formal charge and no lone pair (a carbocation) has how many bonds?
why: It has only six valence electrons around it: three bonds.

stem: A carbon atom has three bonds and one lone pair. What is its formal charge?
why: Three bonds plus a lone pair gives five valence electrons, one more than neutral carbon.

stem: Which structure contains a carbocation?
why: Only the first has a carbon with three bonds and no lone pair (positive charge).

stem: How many hydrogen atoms are bonded to the charged carbon in this ion?
why: The charged carbon is bonded to three methyl groups and a lone pair, so it has no hydrogens.

stem: Draw the methyl cation. How many bonds and lone pairs does the carbon have?
why: A carbocation carbon has three bonds and an empty p orbital.
a: Three bonds and no lone pairs; formal charge +1.

stem: A carbon atom with three bonds can be either positive or negative. How can you tell which?
why: Formal charge depends on the electrons assigned to the carbon.
a: Count the lone pairs: three bonds and no lone pair is positive (+1); three bonds and one lone pair is negative (-1).

stem: State the formal charge on the terminal CH₂ carbon of this ion and the number of lone pairs on it.
why: It has three bonds (two to H, one to C) and a lone pair.

stem: How many lone pairs are on the oxygen atom of an alcohol (R-OH)?
why: Oxygen has six valence electrons: two shared in bonds and four as two lone pairs.

stem: How many lone pairs does the nitrogen atom of a neutral amine (R₃N) have?
why: Nitrogen has five valence electrons: three form bonds and two remain as one lone pair.

stem: Which atom in this compound has two lone pairs?
why: The carbonyl oxygen has two lone pairs; the nitrogen has one.

o.v: Both the oxygen and the nitrogen

stem: How many lone pairs are on all the atoms of acetic acid, CH₃CO₂H?
why: The carbonyl oxygen has two lone pairs and the hydroxyl oxygen has two.

stem: How many lone pairs does the chlorine atom in CH₃Cl have?
why: Chlorine has seven valence electrons: one forms the bond and six form three lone pairs.

stem: Redraw the compound showing all lone pairs. How many are there?
why: Ether oxygen forms two bonds and keeps two lone pairs.
a: Two lone pairs, both on the oxygen.

stem: How many lone pairs are on all the heteroatoms of the compound shown?
why: Each neutral oxygen with two bonds (or a double bond) has two lone pairs.
a: Four: two on the carbonyl oxygen and two on the other oxygen.

stem: Lone pairs are usually not drawn in bond-line structures. Why is it still important to recognize them?
why: They determine how the molecule reacts even when not drawn.
a: Lone pairs make atoms basic and nucleophilic and take part in resonance, so they must be known when predicting reactivity.

stem: In a bond-line drawing, what does a dashed bond indicate?
why: A dash points away from the viewer.

o.v: The group is in front of the plane of the page
The group is behind the plane of the page
The bond is a double bond

stem: In a bond-line drawing, what does a solid wedge indicate?
why: A wedge points toward the viewer.

o.v: The group is in front of the plane of the page
The group is behind the plane of the page
The bond is a triple bond

stem: A tetrahedral carbon is drawn with two bonds in the plane, one on a wedge and one on a dash. Where are the groups on the wedge and the dash?
why: Wedge: toward; dash: away; two plain bonds lie in the plane of the page.

o.v: The wedge group points toward the viewer and the dash group points away
Both point away from the viewer
Both lie in the plane of the page

stem: In the drawing shown, the methyl group is drawn on a wedge. Where is that group relative to the plane of the page?
why: A solid wedge means toward the viewer.

o.v: Toward the viewer (in front of the page)
In the plane of the page

stem: What do a plain bond, a solid wedge and a dashed bond mean in a three-dimensional bond-line structure?
why: These three bond types let a flat drawing show tetrahedral geometry.
a: A plain bond lies in the plane of the page, a wedge comes toward the viewer, and a dash goes away from the viewer.

stem: Describe the position of the methyl group in the drawing shown, relative to the plane of the page.
why: Wedge means toward and dash means away from the viewer.
a: It is drawn on a dash, so it points away from the viewer.

stem: One student draws CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃ with the OH group on a wedge; another draws it on a dash. Are these the same molecule? Explain.
why: Swapping the wedge and dash at the only stereocenter gives the mirror-image arrangement.
a: No. They are mirror images that cannot be superimposed (enantiomers).

stem: Name two drawing styles other than wedge-and-dash that show three-dimensional structure.
why: Both are covered in Section 2.6 of the text.

stem: Which arrow is placed between resonance structures?
why: Resonance structures are connected by a double-headed straight arrow and enclosed in brackets.

stem: Which statement about a resonance hybrid is correct?
why: Resonance structures are drawing tools; the real molecule is one hybrid.

o.v: The molecule rapidly flips between the resonance structures
It is a single species that is a combination of all the resonance structures
Only the most stable resonance structure actually exists
Each resonance structure is a separate isomer

stem: Why is a single bond-line structure inadequate for acetate, CH₃CO₂⁻?
why: The charge and double bond are delocalized over both oxygens, so resonance is needed.

o.v: It does not show the carbon atoms
It shows one C=O and one C-O⁻ bond, but the two carbon-oxygen bonds are actually equivalent
It places the negative charge on carbon

stem: What do the brackets and the double-headed arrow mean when they surround a set of structures?
why: The double-headed arrow is reserved for resonance.
a: The structures are resonance structures of one species, not different molecules in equilibrium.

stem: Is resonance an equilibrium between the resonance structures? Explain.
why: Equilibrium involves different species converting; resonance describes one species.
a: No. The molecule is a single hybrid; resonance structures do not interconvert.

stem: Define resonance stabilization.
why: Delocalized electrons are more stable than localized ones.
a: The lowering of energy that comes from delocalizing electrons over more than one atom through resonance.

stem: In resonance structures, curved arrows show the movement of what?
why: Each curved arrow shows the movement of one electron pair.

stem: Where should the tail of a curved arrow start?
why: The tail marks the source electrons.

o.v: On the nucleus of an atom
On a lone pair or a π bond

stem: Which is NOT allowed when drawing resonance arrows?
why: Resonance moves lone pairs and π bonds, never σ bonds, and never exceeds an octet for second-row elements.

o.v: Moving a lone pair to form a π bond
Moving a π bond onto an adjacent atom
Moving a π bond to become a lone pair

stem: Which set of curved arrows correctly converts this resonance structure of acetate into the other one?
why: Arrow 1 moves a lone pair of O⁻ to form the C=O π bond; arrow 2 moves the old π bond onto the other oxygen as a lone pair.

stem: Draw curved arrow(s) to convert the allyl cation resonance structure shown into the other one.
why: The π bond moves toward the cation, forming a new π bond and leaving a cation at the other end.
a: One curved arrow from the C=C π bond to the space between the C⁺ and its neighbouring carbon, forming a new π bond and moving the positive charge.

stem: Why can a curved arrow not be drawn starting from a single bond in resonance?
why: Resonance structures differ only in electron positions, not atom positions.
a: Resonance moves only π bonds and lone pairs. Breaking a single (σ) bond would change the connectivity of the atoms, which is not resonance.

stem: How many curved arrows are needed to convert one resonance structure of acetate into the other? Describe where each starts and ends.
why: One arrow forms a new π bond and the other pushes the old π bond onto oxygen.
a: Two: a lone pair on the O⁻ forms a C=O π bond, and the original C=O π bond becomes a lone pair on the other oxygen.

stem: A curved arrow starts on the π bond of a C=O group and points to oxygen. Describe the resulting structure.
why: The two π electrons move onto the more electronegative oxygen.
a: Oxygen gains a lone pair (becoming O⁻) and the carbon loses the π bond (becoming C⁺).

stem: What is the formal charge on the oxygen atom that has one single bond and three lone pairs?
why: Six valence electrons minus seven assigned electrons gives -1.

stem: What is the formal charge on nitrogen in the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺?
why: Four bonds and no lone pair gives five minus four electrons: +1.

stem: The ion CH₂=CH-O⁻ has a second resonance structure. On which atom is the negative charge in it?
why: The oxygen lone pair forms a C=O bond and the C=C π electrons end up as a lone pair on the terminal carbon.

o.v: Neither; the second structure is neutral

stem: What is the formal charge on an oxygen atom that has three bonds and one lone pair?
why: Six valence electrons minus (2 + 3) = +1, as in H₃O⁺.

stem: Draw the second resonance structure of the ion shown, including formal charges.
why: Use two curved arrows: a lone pair from O forms C=O and the C=C π bond moves to carbon.
a: The negative charge moves to the terminal carbon: ⁻CH₂-CH=O.

stem: Must the total charge be the same in every resonance structure of an ion? Explain.
why: Electrons are moved, not added or removed.
a: Yes. Resonance only moves electrons, so the overall charge is unchanged; the individual formal charges may move.

stem: Which of these is NOT one of the five patterns used to find resonance structures?
why: Without a lone pair, positive charge or conjugated π system next to it, a double bond cannot delocalize.

o.v: An isolated double bond with no adjacent lone pair or charge
Conjugated π bonds in a ring

stem: Which anion has an allylic lone pair and can therefore be drawn with resonance?
why: The lone pair on carbon is adjacent to the C=C π bond.

stem: How many resonance structures (including the one drawn) are there for the allyl cation, CH₂=CH-CH₂⁺?
why: Moving the π bond swaps the positions of the double bond and the positive charge.

stem: How many resonance structures with alternating double bonds can be drawn for benzene?
why: Two Kekulé structures differ in the placement of the three double bonds.

stem: Which resonance pattern applies to acetate?
why: The lone pair on O⁻ is adjacent to the C=O π bond.

o.v: An allylic lone pair (a lone pair next to a π bond)
A lone pair adjacent to a carbocation
Conjugated π bonds in a ring

stem: Draw both resonance structures of the allyl anion.
why: Pattern 1: an allylic lone pair; one curved arrow from the lone pair and one from the π bond.

stem: Draw the second resonance structure of the allyl cation.
why: Pattern 2: an allylic carbocation; the π bond shifts toward the positive carbon.

stem: Draw a resonance structure of acrolein, CH₂=CH-CH=O, in which oxygen carries a negative charge.
why: Pattern 4 (a π bond between atoms of different electronegativity) combined with conjugation: the π electrons move onto oxygen.

stem: Draw the resonance structure of CH₃-O-CH₂⁺ that places the positive charge on oxygen. Which pattern is this?
why: The oxygen lone pair forms a π bond to the carbon.
a: CH₃-O⁺=CH₂; pattern 3, a lone pair adjacent to a carbocation.

stem: How many resonance structures can be drawn for the phenoxide ion (including both Kekulé forms)? On which atoms can the negative charge be placed?
why: The oxygen lone pair is adjacent to the ring π system, so charge moves to the ortho and para positions (not meta).
a: Five structures: the negative charge can be on the oxygen, on either ortho carbon, or on the para carbon; the oxygen form can be drawn with either Kekulé arrangement.

stem: Which resonance structures contribute equally to the resonance hybrid?
why: Equivalent resonance forms have identical charge placement and bonding patterns.

o.v: Structures with the fewest filled octets
Structures that are equally good Lewis structures (equivalent)

stem: Which resonance structure is the more significant contributor?
why: Other things being equal, a negative charge is better on oxygen than on carbon.

o.v: II, because the negative charge is on carbon
I, because the negative charge is on the more electronegative atom (oxygen)
II, because it has fewer formal charges

stem: Are the two resonance structures of acetate equivalent?
why: Each oxygen carries the charge in one structure and the double bond in the other.

o.v: No, one has a negative charge on carbon
Yes, both have a negative charge on one oxygen and a C=O on the other
No, one has no formal charge
No, one has an incomplete octet

stem: Which resonance structure of the methoxymethyl cation is more significant?
why: The carbon in structure I has only six electrons; in II all atoms have octets (the first rule).

o.v: I, because the positive charge is on carbon
I, because it has fewer bonds
II, because every atom has a complete octet

stem: State the first and second rules used to decide which resonance structure is more significant.
why: These are two of the four rules in Section 2.11.
a: First, the structure with the greatest number of filled octets is more significant. Second, the structure with fewer formal charges is more significant.

stem: Why is a resonance structure with separated positive and negative charges usually less significant than one without charges?
why: Rule 2: fewer formal charges.
a: Charge separation costs energy, and structures with fewer formal charges are more significant.

stem: Of the two resonance structures of the enolate shown, which contributes more to the hybrid and why?
why: A negative charge is more stable on the more electronegative atom.
a: The one with the negative charge on oxygen (I), because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon.

stem: List the four guidelines for judging the significance of resonance structures.
why: These are the rules in Section 2.11.
a: (1) Most filled octets; (2) fewest formal charges; (3) negative charge on the more electronegative atom (positive on the less); (4) equally good structures contribute equally.

stem: How is a resonance hybrid drawn?
why: Partial bonds and partial charges show the delocalization.

o.v: With two structures and an equilibrium arrow
With the most stable structure only
With a double bond on each side
With dashed (partial) bonds and partial charges (δ)

stem: What is the carbon-oxygen bond order in each C-O bond of acetate?
why: The two oxygens are equivalent: each C-O bond is between a single and a double bond.

stem: Describe how the resonance hybrid of the allyl cation is drawn.
why: The positive charge is shared equally by the two terminal carbons.
a: Both carbon-carbon bonds are drawn as dashed partial double bonds, and each terminal carbon carries a partial positive charge (δ+).

stem: In the resonance hybrid of acetate, what is the charge on each oxygen?
why: The one negative charge is shared by two equivalent oxygens.
a: Each oxygen carries half of the negative charge (about -1/2, written δ⁻).

stem: In an amide, the lone pair on nitrogen is:
why: A lone pair next to a π bond can participate in resonance and occupies a p orbital.

o.v: Delocalized, because it is in an s orbital
Delocalized, because it is adjacent to the C=O π bond

stem: Compare the nitrogen lone pair in CH₃CH₂NH₂ and in CH₂=CHNH₂.
why: Only the vinyl amine has a lone pair adjacent to a π bond.

o.v: Delocalized in the first and localized in the second
Localized in the first and delocalized in the second

stem: A carbonyl oxygen has a π bond and lone pairs. Which statement is correct?
why: An atom with both a π bond and a lone pair uses only one of them in resonance (the π bond).

o.v: The lone pairs and the π bond both participate in resonance
Neither the lone pairs nor the π bond can participate
The lone pairs participate but the π bond does not
The π bond can participate in resonance but the lone pairs on that oxygen do not

stem: In the ester shown, identify the oxygen lone pair that is delocalized and say why.
why: The carbonyl oxygen lone pairs are localized (in sp² orbitals).
a: The lone pair on the single-bonded oxygen is delocalized because it is adjacent to the C=O π bond.

stem: Is the nitrogen lone pair in aniline localized or delocalized? Explain.
why: The lone pair occupies a p orbital that overlaps with the ring π bonds.
a: Delocalized: it is adjacent to the π system of the ring, so it participates in resonance.

stem: Draw the resonance structure of the amide shown that results from delocalizing the nitrogen lone pair.
why: This is pattern 1 combined with the polarized C=O.
a: CH₃C(O⁻)=NH₂⁺: the nitrogen lone pair forms a C=N π bond and the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen.

stem: In the reaction HCl + H₂O ⇌ Cl⁻ + H₃O⁺, which species is the conjugate base of HCl?
why: The conjugate base is what remains after the acid loses a proton.

stem: In which reaction does water act as an acid?
why: Only in the first reaction does water donate a proton (becoming HO⁻); in the others it accepts one.

stem: Define a Brønsted-Lowry acid and a Brønsted-Lowry base.
why: The definition is based on the transfer of a proton.
a: An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor.

stem: In NH₃ + HCl → NH₄⁺ + Cl⁻, identify the acid, base, conjugate acid and conjugate base.
why: HCl donates the proton to NH₃.
a: Acid: HCl; base: NH₃; conjugate acid: NH₄⁺; conjugate base: Cl⁻.

stem: Water can act as an acid or as a base. Write one reaction for each and name the conjugate partner formed.
why: Water is amphoteric.
a: As a base: HCl + H₂O → Cl⁻ + H₃O⁺ (conjugate acid H₃O⁺). As an acid: CH₃O⁻ + H₂O → CH₃OH + HO⁻ (conjugate base HO⁻).

stem: Give the conjugate acid of CH₃NH₂ and the conjugate base of CH₃OH.
why: Add a proton to the base; remove a proton from the acid.
a: The conjugate acid of CH₃NH₂ is CH₃NH₃⁺; the conjugate base of CH₃OH is CH₃O⁻.

stem: What is the minimum number of curved arrows needed to show a proton transfer?
why: One arrow shows the base attacking the proton and a second shows the X-H bond breaking.

stem: Which curved arrows correctly show hydroxide removing a proton from HCl?
why: Arrow 1 starts on a lone pair of the base and ends on the proton; arrow 2 starts on the H-Cl bond and ends on chlorine.

stem: Draw the curved arrows for the reaction of hydroxide with HCl.
why: Tail on the electron source, head on where the electrons go.
a: Arrow 1: from a lone pair on HO⁻ to the hydrogen of HCl. Arrow 2: from the H-Cl bond to the chlorine atom, giving H₂O and Cl⁻.

stem: Why does every proton transfer need at least two curved arrows?
why: A hydrogen cannot hold more than one bond.
a: One arrow shows the base forming a bond to the proton and a second shows the bond to the proton breaking, so the proton is never left with two bonds.

stem: Describe the curved arrows for CH₃CO₂H reacting with hydroxide, including where each arrow starts and ends.
why: The base attacks the proton and the O-H bond electrons move onto oxygen.
a: Arrow 1: from a lone pair on HO⁻ to the acidic hydrogen. Arrow 2: from the O-H bond of the acid to its oxygen atom, forming CH₃CO₂⁻ and H₂O.

stem: For NH₃ + HBr, state where the tail and head of each curved arrow are placed.
why: Lone pair attacks the proton; the H-Br bond leaves with its electrons.
a: Arrow 1 starts on the nitrogen lone pair and ends on the H of HBr. Arrow 2 starts on the H-Br bond and ends on bromine, forming NH₄⁺ and Br⁻.

stem: Which acid is stronger: one with pKa 4.75 or one with pKa 15.7?
why: A lower pKa means a stronger acid.

o.v: It depends on the solvent only

stem: Acid A has pKa 5 and acid B has pKa 9. How many times more acidic is A than B?
why: Each pKa unit is a factor of ten, so four units is 10⁴.

stem: For CH₃CO₂H + HO⁻ ⇌ CH₃CO₂⁻ + H₂O (pKa of CH₃CO₂H = 4.75; pKa of H₂O = 15.7), which side is favored?
why: Equilibrium favors the weaker acid, water (higher pKa).

stem: Which is more acidic, ethanol (pKa 16) or acetic acid (pKa 4.75)? By about how many orders of magnitude?
why: 16 - 4.75 is roughly 11 pKa units.
a: Acetic acid is more acidic, by about 11 orders of magnitude.

stem: Use pKa values to rank from weakest to strongest acid: NH₃ (38), HC≡CH (25), H₂O (15.7).
why: The higher the pKa, the weaker the acid.

stem: Predict the position of the equilibrium HC≡CH + NH₂⁻ ⇌ HC≡C⁻ + NH₃ (pKa of HC≡CH = 25; pKa of NH₃ = 38).
why: Equilibrium favors the weaker acid.
a: The products are favored, because NH₃ (pKa 38) is the weaker acid.

stem: Rank HO⁻, CH₃CO₂⁻ and NH₂⁻ from weakest to strongest base. (Conjugate acid pKa values: H₂O 15.7, CH₃CO₂H 4.75, NH₃ 38.)
why: The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the base.

stem: The pKa of H₃O⁺ is -1.74 and that of NH₄⁺ is 9.3. Which is the stronger base, H₂O or NH₃? Explain.
why: A weak acid has a strong conjugate base.
a: NH₃ is the stronger base, because its conjugate acid (NH₄⁺) is the weaker acid.

stem: HA has pKa 15 and HB has pKa 5. Which side is favored in A⁻ + HB ⇌ HA + B⁻? Explain.
why: The stronger acid reacts with the stronger base.
a: The products. HB is the stronger acid, so the equilibrium favors the weaker acid (HA) and the weaker base (B⁻).

stem: Which is the stronger acid, HF or HCl?
why: Within a column, size beats electronegativity.

o.v: HF, because F is more electronegative
HCl, because Cl⁻ is larger and spreads the charge over more space

stem: Which compound is the stronger acid?
why: The electron-withdrawing CF₃ group stabilizes the negative charge of the conjugate base.

o.v: CH₃CH₂OH, because it has fewer halogens
CF₃CH₂OH, because the fluorines stabilize the alkoxide by induction
CH₃CH₂OH, because its oxygen is more electronegative

stem: Which hydrogen is the most acidic?
why: An sp orbital holds the negative charge closer to the nucleus.

o.v: The H on the sp carbon (the alkyne C-H)
The H on the sp² carbon
A H on the CH₃ group

stem: Which is more acidic, H₂O or H₂S? Explain.
why: Compare atoms in the same column by size.
a: H₂S, because S is larger than O, so HS⁻ spreads its charge over a larger volume.

stem: Which is more acidic, NH₃ or H₂O? Explain.
why: Same row: electronegativity decides.
a: H₂O, because oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen and stabilizes the negative charge of HO⁻ better.

stem: Which is more acidic, CH₃OH or CH₃SH? Explain.
why: O and S are in the same column.
a: CH₃SH, because CH₃S⁻ is larger than CH₃O⁻ and stabilizes charge better (size dominates within a column).

stem: Which is more acidic, ethanol or acetic acid? Explain using the conjugate bases.
why: Both charges are on oxygen, so compare resonance.
a: Acetic acid; the acetate ion is stabilized by resonance (charge on two oxygens), but ethoxide has a localized charge.

stem: Which N-H is more acidic, the amide N-H or the amine N-H? Explain.
why: Both charges are on nitrogen, so compare resonance.
a: The amide N-H; its conjugate base has the charge delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen by resonance.

stem: Phenol is a stronger acid than cyclohexanol. Explain using the conjugate bases.
why: Both anions have the charge on oxygen.
a: Phenoxide is stabilized by resonance (the negative charge delocalizes onto ortho and para carbons), but cyclohexoxide has a localized charge.

stem: Which is the stronger acid, CH₃CO₂H or ClCH₂CO₂H? Explain.
why: Same atom and resonance; induction differs.
a: ClCH₂CO₂H; the electronegative chlorine withdraws electron density through the σ bonds (induction) and stabilizes the carboxylate.

stem: Which is the stronger acid: 2-chlorobutanoic acid or 4-chlorobutanoic acid? Explain.
why: Induction decreases as the number of bonds between Cl and the acid group increases.
a: 2-Chlorobutanoic acid, because the chlorine is closer to the carboxylate and the inductive effect weakens with distance.

stem: Which O-H is more acidic in this compound? Explain.
why: Compare the inductive effect near each alkoxide.
a: The O-H on the carbon bearing the two CF₃ groups; the six fluorines stabilize that alkoxide by induction.

stem: Which is more acidic, ethane or ethyne? Explain.
why: sp > sp² > sp³ for stabilizing a negative charge.
a: Ethyne; its conjugate base has the charge in an sp orbital, which is closer to the nucleus and more stable.

stem: In 1-butene-3-yne only one hydrogen is much more acidic than the others. Which hydrogen is it and why?
why: Compare sp, sp² and sp³ carbon-hydrogen bonds.
a: The alkyne hydrogen on the sp carbon; the conjugate base has its charge in an sp orbital.

stem: Explain why an sp orbital stabilizes a negative charge better than an sp³ orbital.
why: More s character means the electrons are closer to the positive nucleus.
a: An sp orbital has 50% s character, and s electrons are held closer to the nucleus than p electrons, so the lone pair is lower in energy.

stem: Which is more acidic, the O-H of propan-1-ol or the C-H of propyne (on the sp carbon)? Name the factor that decides.
why: Order of priority: atom, resonance, induction, orbital.
a: The O-H, because the atom (O versus C) takes priority over the orbital effect.

stem: Which O-H is more acidic in this compound? Explain which factor wins.
why: Atom ties; resonance outranks induction.
a: The carboxylic acid O-H; resonance (a delocalized carboxylate) is more important than the inductive effect of the nearby CCl₃ group.

stem: Which C-H is more acidic: the CH₂ between two carbonyls in CH₃COCH₂COCH₃, or the terminal alkyne C-H in HC≡CH? Explain.
why: Both are carbon acids; resonance outranks orbitals.
a: The CH₂ between the carbonyls; its conjugate base is resonance stabilized (charge on two oxygens), which outranks the orbital effect.

stem: Rank from least to most acidic and explain: I = HC≡CH, II = CH₃CH₂OH, III = CH₃COCH₂COCH₃ (central CH₂).
why: Compare the conjugate bases using atom, resonance, induction and orbital in order.
a: I < II < III. Acetylene is a carbon acid (an sp carbanion); ethanol puts the charge on oxygen (atom beats orbital); the diketone anion is resonance stabilized (charge on two oxygens), which outranks atom alone.

stem: Which is the stronger acid, NH₄⁺ or H₃O⁺?
why: A positive charge is more stable on the less electronegative atom.

o.v: NH₄⁺, because nitrogen is less electronegative
H₃O⁺, because oxygen is less able than nitrogen to stabilize a positive charge
NH₄⁺, because it has more hydrogens

stem: Which is the stronger base, CH₃NH₂ or CH₃OH?
why: Nitrogen holds a positive charge better than oxygen, so the amine is more easily protonated.

stem: Aniline is a weaker base than methylamine because:
why: A delocalized lone pair is less available to accept a proton.

o.v: The nitrogen lone pair of aniline is delocalized into the ring
Nitrogen in aniline is less electronegative
The ring is electron donating by induction only

stem: Draw the conjugate acid of CH₃CH₂NH₂. Which atom carries the positive charge?
why: Protonate the nitrogen lone pair.
a: CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺; the nitrogen carries the positive charge.

stem: Why are amines stronger bases than alcohols?
why: Compare the stability of the conjugate acids.
a: Nitrogen is less electronegative than oxygen, so a positive charge on nitrogen (the conjugate acid) is more stable than on oxygen.

stem: Explain why amides are extremely poor bases.
why: A delocalized lone pair is a weak base.
a: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen by resonance, so it is not available to accept a proton.

stem: Which is the stronger acid, CH₃NH₃⁺ (pKa 10.6) or C₆H₅NH₃⁺ (pKa 4.6)? Explain using the conjugate bases.
why: Strong acid means weak conjugate base.
a: C₆H₅NH₃⁺; its conjugate base (aniline) has a lone pair delocalized into the ring, making it the weaker base.

stem: Draw the product of protonating pyridine and state which atom is protonated.
why: The nitrogen lone pair lies in the plane of the ring, not in the π system.
a: The nitrogen is protonated, giving the pyridinium ion.

stem: Which side is favored in NH₂⁻ + CH₃OH ⇌ NH₃ + CH₃O⁻?
why: Equilibrium favors the more stable anion: O⁻ is more stable than N⁻ (same row).

stem: Is water a suitable proton source to convert the acetate ion into acetic acid?
why: H₂O + CH₃CO₂⁻ → CH₃CO₂H + HO⁻ is uphill; a stronger acid such as H₃O⁺ is needed.

o.v: Yes; water is a strong acid
Yes; the equilibrium favors acetic acid
No, because water has no protons
No; the equilibrium favors acetate because it is a resonance-stabilized, weaker base than HO⁻

stem: Predict the position of equilibrium: CH₃CO₂⁻ + HCl ⇌ CH₃CO₂H + Cl⁻.
why: HCl is the stronger acid.
a: The products are favored, because Cl⁻ is a much weaker base than acetate.

stem: Is hydroxide a strong enough base to deprotonate phenol? Explain.
why: The equilibrium favors the more stable anion.
a: Yes. Phenoxide is resonance stabilized, so phenol (pKa 9.9) is a stronger acid than water (15.7) and the equilibrium favors phenoxide.

stem: A student wants to convert CH₃CH₂OH completely into its alkoxide. Is NaOH or NaNH₂ the better choice? Explain.
why: Compare the conjugate acids of the two bases.
a: NaNH₂. Ethanol (pKa 16) and water (15.7) have similar acidity, so NaOH gives only a partial equilibrium, whereas NH₂⁻ is a far stronger base (NH₃ pKa 38) and deprotonates ethanol completely.

stem: Is water a suitable proton source to protonate CH₃CH₂O⁻? Explain.
why: Compare the acidities of water and ethanol.
a: Yes. Water (pKa 15.7) is about as acidic as ethanol (16), so the equilibrium lies roughly in balance and favors the alcohol with excess water.

stem: Is hydroxide a suitable base to deprotonate acetylene? Explain.
why: Equilibrium favors the weaker acid.
a: No. Acetylene (pKa 25) is far less acidic than water (15.7), so the equilibrium favors the reactants. A base such as NH₂⁻ is needed.

stem: What is the strongest base that can exist in water?
why: Any base stronger than HO⁻ reacts with water to give HO⁻ (the leveling effect).

stem: What happens when sodium amide (NaNH₂) is added to water?
why: NH₂⁻ is a stronger base than HO⁻, so it is destroyed by the solvent.

o.v: It reacts with water to give NH₃ and HO⁻

stem: State the leveling effect for bases in a solvent.
why: In water the limit is HO⁻.
a: The strongest base that can exist in a solvent is the conjugate base of the solvent; any stronger base reacts with the solvent.

stem: Why can NaNH₂ not be used as a base in water, and what solvent could be used instead?
why: Choose a solvent whose conjugate base is at least as strong as the base.
a: NH₂⁻ deprotonates water, giving HO⁻. Liquid ammonia (or a solvent such as THF) can be used because it is not deprotonated.

stem: What is the strongest acid that can exist in water?
why: The leveling effect applies to acids as well.
a: H₃O⁺; a stronger acid such as HCl simply protonates water to form H₃O⁺.

stem: Why is the tert-butoxide ion less stable than the ethoxide ion in solution?
why: Steric hindrance reduces solvation.

o.v: It has a smaller negative charge
It is bulky, so solvent molecules cannot approach and stabilize the negative oxygen as well

stem: Ethanol (pKa 16) is slightly more acidic than tert-butanol (pKa 18). Explain.
why: Solvation depends on how well solvent molecules reach the charge.
a: Ethoxide is better solvated than the sterically hindered tert-butoxide, so it is more stable and ethanol is the stronger acid.

stem: Predict which is the stronger base, CH₃O⁻ or (CH₃)₃CO⁻, and explain how solvation contributes.
why: Less stabilized means a stronger base.
a: (CH₃)₃CO⁻ is stronger, because the bulky groups hinder solvation of its negative charge, leaving it less stabilized.

stem: In the reagent NaOH, which ion acts as the base?
why: The sodium counterion is a spectator.

stem: What is a counterion?
why: It is also called a spectator ion.
a: A positively charged species (such as Na⁺, K⁺, Li⁺) that accompanies a negatively charged base; it usually does not take part in the reaction.

stem: Rewrite NaNH₂ + H₂O → NH₃ + NaOH without the counterion.
why: Na⁺ is a spectator.

stem: Which species is a Lewis acid?
why: BF₃ has an empty p orbital and accepts an electron pair.

stem: In BF₃ + O(CH₃)₂ → F₃B⁻-O⁺(CH₃)₂, identify the Lewis acid and the Lewis base.
why: The oxygen lone pair is donated to boron.
a: BF₃ is the Lewis acid (electron-pair acceptor); dimethyl ether is the Lewis base (electron-pair donor).

stem: BF₃ has no hydrogens. Explain how it can still be an acid.
why: Lewis acidity is defined by electron-pair acceptance, not proton donation.
a: It is a Lewis acid: boron has an empty p orbital and accepts an electron pair.

stem: How many curved arrows are needed for NH₃ + BF₃ → H₃N⁺-B⁻F₃? Draw it.
why: A Lewis acid-base reaction forms one new bond, so one arrow is enough.
a: One: from the nitrogen lone pair to boron.

stem: What is the general molecular formula of an acyclic alkane with n carbon atoms?
why: Saturated acyclic hydrocarbons have two hydrogens per carbon plus two more at the chain ends.

stem: Which compound is a saturated hydrocarbon?
why: A saturated hydrocarbon has no π bonds; the others contain C=C or C≡C bonds.

stem: Give the molecular formula of the unbranched alkane that has eight carbon atoms.
why: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ with n = 8.

stem: How many hydrogen atoms does cyclohexane have, and why is this two fewer than hexane?
why: Cycloalkanes have the formula CₙH₂ₙ.
a: Cyclohexane is C₆H₁₂. Closing the ring removes one hydrogen from each end carbon (two hydrogens in total).

stem: What is the IUPAC parent name for an unbranched chain of six carbon atoms?
why: The prefixes are meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-, hept-, oct-, non-, dec-.

why: Find the longest continuous chain of carbons, not just the one drawn horizontally.

stem: Draw 2,3-dimethylbutane.

a: A four-carbon chain with a methyl group on each of carbons 2 and 3.

stem: What are the names of the substituents -CH(CH₃)₂ and -C(CH₃)₃?
why: These common names for complex substituents are accepted by IUPAC.

stem: A student names the compound shown 2-ethylbutane. Explain the mistake and give the correct name.
why: Always choose the longest continuous chain as the parent.
a: The longest chain has five carbons, not four. The correct name is 3-methylpentane.

stem: How many constitutional isomers does pentane (C₅H₁₂) have?
why: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

stem: Which pair are constitutional isomers?
why: Both are C₄H₁₀ with different connectivity; the others differ in molecular formula.

stem: Draw all constitutional isomers of C₅H₁₂ and name them.
why: Vary the longest chain: five carbons, four carbons plus a methyl, three carbons plus two methyls.

stem: Draw all five constitutional isomers of C₆H₁₄.
why: Work systematically from the longest chain downward and avoid drawing the same compound twice.

stem: Are the two drawings the same compound? Explain.
why: Compare the connectivity, not the orientation.
a: Yes. Both are a four-carbon chain with a methyl group on carbon 2 (2-methylbutane); numbering from the other end only changes how it is drawn.

stem: Two isomeric alkanes are burned. The isomer with the smaller heat of combustion is:
why: Less energy released means the starting alkane was already lower in energy.

o.v: The one with more carbon atoms
The one with fewer hydrogen atoms

stem: Compared with their unbranched isomers, branched alkanes are generally:
why: Branching lowers the energy of an alkane.

o.v: More stable, with lower heats of combustion
Less stable, with higher heats of combustion
More stable, with higher heats of combustion

stem: Define the heat of combustion of an alkane.
why: It can be measured and used to compare isomers.
a: The heat released (-ΔH°) when one mole of the alkane burns completely in oxygen.

stem: Octane and 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane are isomers (C₈H₁₈). Which has the smaller heat of combustion? Explain.
why: Both give the same products, so differences in heat come from differences in starting energy.
a: 2,2,3,3-Tetramethylbutane, because the more highly branched isomer is more stable and releases less heat.

stem: What process separates crude oil into fractions?
why: Fractions are separated by differences in boiling point.

stem: Which process converts straight-chain alkanes into branched and aromatic hydrocarbons that reduce knocking?
why: Cracking breaks large alkanes into smaller ones; reforming rearranges them.

stem: Distinguish cracking from reforming.
why: Both improve the yield and quality of gasoline.
a: Cracking breaks C-C bonds of large alkanes to make smaller alkanes suitable for gasoline. Reforming converts straight-chain alkanes into branched and aromatic hydrocarbons that burn more smoothly.

stem: Why do petroleum fractions come off a distillation tower at different temperatures?
why: Larger alkanes have stronger dispersion forces.
a: They have different boiling points, and boiling points increase with molecular size.

stem: In a Newman projection, what does the circle represent?
why: The front carbon is the point where the front bonds meet; the circle is the back carbon.

o.v: The back carbon, with its bonds starting at the circle

stem: What kind of conformation of ethane is shown?
why: The front and back C-H bonds are 60° apart.

stem: This Newman projection looks down the C2-C3 bond of butane. What is the conformation?
why: The two CH₃ groups are 180° apart.

stem: Draw a staggered Newman projection of ethane.
why: Staggered means the groups are 60° apart.
a: The front carbon has three C-H bonds meeting at the center; the back carbon (a circle) has three C-H bonds placed between the front bonds.

stem: How do you read a Newman projection?
why: The two carbons are one behind the other.
a: You look straight down one C-C bond. The front carbon is the point where three bonds meet and the back carbon is the circle with three bonds starting at its edge.

stem: Draw a staggered Newman projection of propane looking down the C1-C2 bond, with the methyl group of C2 on the back carbon.
why: C2 carries the CH₃ group.
a: The front carbon (C1) shows three hydrogens; the back carbon (C2) shows CH₃ and two hydrogens, each between front bonds.

stem: Which conformation of ethane is lower in energy?
why: Staggered C-H bonds are farthest apart.

stem: The energy cost of eclipsing in ethane is called:
why: Torsional strain comes from eclipsing interactions between bonds.

stem: How does the torsional strain of propane (eclipsed) compare with that of ethane?
why: The extra methyl group adds a small amount of strain to the eclipsed form.

o.v: Slightly larger, because a C-H bond eclipses a C-CH₃ bond

stem: Sketch the energy diagram for one full 360° rotation about the C-C bond of ethane. How many maxima and minima does it have?
why: Staggered and eclipsed conformations alternate every 60°.
a: Three minima (staggered) and three maxima (eclipsed), repeating every 60°.

stem: What is the dihedral angle between a front group and the nearest back group in a staggered conformation and in an eclipsed conformation?
why: The dihedral (torsional) angle measures the relative position of front and back groups.

stem: Define torsional strain.
why: It is largest when the dihedral angle is zero.
a: The increase in energy of a molecule caused by eclipsing interactions between bonds on adjacent atoms.

stem: Why are all three staggered conformations of ethane equal in energy?
why: Equivalent structures have identical energy.
a: Each carbon has three identical hydrogens, so rotating by 120° gives an arrangement that is indistinguishable from the first (they are degenerate).

stem: Which Newman projection shows the most stable conformation of butane (looking down the C2-C3 bond)?
why: The anti conformation keeps the two CH₃ groups as far apart as possible (180°).

stem: Which conformation of butane is the highest in energy?
why: Eclipsing of the two methyl groups gives both torsional and steric strain.

o.v: The one in which the two CH₃ groups eclipse each other

stem: Why is the gauche conformation of butane higher in energy than the anti conformation?
why: Both are staggered, so the difference is the van der Waals crowding of the methyl groups.

o.v: Steric strain: the two CH₃ groups are only 60° apart and crowd each other
The gauche form has an extra bond

stem: Which list orders the butane conformations from lowest to highest energy?
why: Staggered forms are below eclipsed forms, and anti is the best staggered form.

stem: Draw the anti conformation of butane as a Newman projection looking down C2-C3.
why: Anti means the dihedral angle between the methyl groups is 180°.
a: Front carbon: CH₃ at the top and two H; back carbon: CH₃ at the bottom (180° from the front CH₃) and two H.

stem: Draw the gauche conformation of butane as a Newman projection looking down C2-C3.
why: Gauche means the dihedral angle between the methyl groups is 60°.
a: The two CH₃ groups are 60° apart (both staggered).

stem: List the four main conformations of butane from lowest to highest energy and explain the order.
why: Torsional and steric strain both contribute.
a: Anti, gauche, eclipsed (CH₃ eclipsing H) and totally eclipsed (CH₃ eclipsing CH₃). Staggered forms avoid torsional strain; anti also avoids steric crowding; the totally eclipsed form has the most strain.

stem: What type of strain is present in the gauche conformation but absent in the anti conformation?
why: Gauche is staggered, so there is no torsional strain.
a: Steric strain, from the two methyl groups being close together.

stem: What is the general formula for a cycloalkane with one ring?
why: Forming the ring removes two hydrogens from CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

stem: Which ring would have the most angle strain if it were planar?
why: Its 60° bond angles deviate most from the tetrahedral 109.5°.

stem: Why does cyclopropane suffer from angle strain?
why: The carbons of a three-membered ring are forced into a triangle.
a: Its C-C-C bond angles are 60°, far from the ideal 109.5° of sp³ carbon.

stem: Draw ethylcyclobutane.
why: Cyclobutane is the parent.
a: A four-membered ring bearing an ethyl substituent.

stem: A planar cyclohexane would have 120° bond angles. Explain why real cyclohexane is not planar.
why: A planar ring would be strained in both ways.
a: It puckers into a chair conformation, which has nearly tetrahedral (109.5°) angles and staggered bonds, relieving angle and torsional strain.

stem: Which conformation of cyclohexane is the most stable?
why: The chair has tetrahedral angles and all bonds staggered.

stem: Which order of cyclohexane conformations is from lowest to highest energy?
why: The chair is the global minimum and the half-chair is the highest-energy transition-state-like form.

stem: The C-C-C bond angles in the chair conformation of cyclohexane are approximately:
why: The chair is essentially free of angle strain.

stem: Explain why the chair conformation has no significant angle or torsional strain.
why: Look at the Newman projection down any ring C-C bond.
a: Its bond angles are close to 109.5° and all neighbouring C-H and C-C bonds are staggered.

stem: Why is the boat conformation higher in energy than the chair?
why: Both torsional and steric strain are present.
a: The boat has eclipsing interactions along its sides and the two flagpole hydrogens crowd each other.

stem: How many axial and how many equatorial hydrogens does the chair of cyclohexane have?
why: Each ring carbon has two hydrogens, one axial and one equatorial.
a: Six axial and six equatorial hydrogens (one of each on every carbon).

stem: Is the CH₃ group in this chair axial or equatorial?
why: It points straight up, parallel to the ring axis.

stem: Is the chlorine in this chair axial or equatorial?
why: It points outward from the ring, roughly parallel to the ring bonds one carbon away.

stem: How can you recognize the axial bonds in a drawing of a chair?
why: Equatorial bonds point outward, roughly in the plane of the ring.
a: Axial bonds are vertical (parallel to the ring axis) and alternate up and down on adjacent carbons.

stem: Draw the chair that results from a ring flip of the conformation shown. Is the CH₃ now axial or equatorial?
why: A ring flip turns every axial group into an equatorial one and vice versa.
a: After the ring flip the CH₃ group is equatorial.

stem: How do axial bonds on adjacent carbons of a chair point?
why: Axial bonds alternate up and down around the ring.
a: In opposite directions: if one axial bond is up, the next is down.

stem: Which chair of methylcyclohexane is more stable?
why: An axial CH₃ crowds the axial hydrogens on carbons 3 and 5.

o.v: The left chair, with CH₃ axial
Neither; the boat is more stable
The right chair, with CH₃ equatorial

stem: The steric interaction between an axial substituent and the axial hydrogens on carbons 3 and 5 is called:
why: The axial group points into the same face as the axial hydrogens two carbons away.

o.v: A gauche interaction in a chain

stem: Why does a substituent prefer the equatorial position on a cyclohexane chair?
why: Compare the number of gauche-type interactions.
a: In the axial position it suffers 1,3-diaxial interactions with the axial hydrogens on the same face of the ring; the equatorial position points away from the ring and avoids them.

stem: Which has the larger preference for the equatorial position, CH₃ or C(CH₃)₃? Explain.
why: The larger the group, the greater the strain when axial.
a: C(CH₃)₃, because the bulky tert-butyl group has much more severe 1,3-diaxial interactions than CH₃.

stem: In methylcyclohexane, about how much more strained is the axial chair than the equatorial chair, and where does the strain come from?
why: Each 1,3-diaxial CH₃/H interaction resembles one gauche interaction in butane.
a: About 7.6 kJ/mol: two gauche-butane-type interactions (about 3.8 kJ/mol each) between the axial CH₃ and the axial hydrogens on carbons 3 and 5.

stem: Which conformation of cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane is more stable?
why: The diaxial chair has a severe CH₃/CH₃ 1,3-diaxial interaction.

o.v: The left chair, with both CH₃ groups axial
The right chair, with both CH₃ groups equatorial
Neither chair; only the boat exists

stem: Which isomer can exist in a chair with both substituents equatorial?
why: The others have one axial and one equatorial group in each chair.

stem: Draw both chair conformations of trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane and state which is more stable.
why: Trans-1,4 substituents are both axial or both equatorial.
a: One chair has both CH₃ groups axial and the other has both equatorial; the diequatorial chair is more stable.

stem: Describe the two chair conformations of cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane. Which is more stable?
why: Cis-1,2 groups are always axial/equatorial.
a: In each chair one CH₃ is axial and one is equatorial, so the two chairs have the same energy.

stem: Draw both chairs of cis-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane. Which interaction makes the diaxial chair very unstable?
why: Cis-1,3 groups are both axial or both equatorial.
a: The two axial CH₃ groups on the same face (carbons 1 and 3) interact strongly with each other (a CH₃/CH₃ 1,3-diaxial interaction), so the diequatorial chair is strongly preferred.

stem: In cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane the two methyl groups are:
why: Cis means same side; trans means opposite sides.

o.v: On opposite faces of the ring
Both in the plane of the ring
On the same face of the ring

stem: Can cis- and trans-1,3-dimethylcyclohexane interconvert by a ring flip?
why: A ring flip changes axial/equatorial, not the faces the groups are on.

o.v: No; they are different stereoisomers that can only interconvert by breaking bonds
Yes, by rotating a C-C bond
Yes, at high temperature without breaking bonds

stem: Draw cis- and trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane using wedges and dashes.
why: Same face is cis; opposite faces is trans.
a: In the cis isomer both methyl groups are on wedges (or both on dashes); in the trans isomer one is on a wedge and one is on a dash.

stem: Why are cis and trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane stereoisomers rather than constitutional isomers?
why: Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity.
a: They have the same connectivity but a different spatial arrangement, and they cannot interconvert without breaking bonds.

stem: Which prefix is used in the name of a compound that contains two rings sharing atoms?
why: Bicycloalkanes are named with "bicyclo" and bracketed bridge lengths.

stem: Name the bicyclic compound shown (two fused six-membered rings, ten carbons).
why: The bracket numbers give the carbons in each bridge between the bridgeheads: 4, 4 and 0.

stem: How many carbons are in the bicyclic compound bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane, and what does the 1 in the brackets tell you?
why: Add the bridge numbers and the two bridgehead carbons: 2 + 2 + 1 + 2 = 7.
a: Seven carbons (2 + 2 + 1 + the two bridgeheads). The 1 is the number of carbons in the shortest bridge between the bridgeheads.

stem: Which term describes two compounds with the same molecular formula but different connectivity of atoms?
why: Constitutional isomers differ in which atoms are bonded to which.

stem: Which term describes two compounds with the same connectivity but a different spatial arrangement of atoms?
why: Same connectivity, different arrangement in space.

stem: What is the relationship between the two compounds shown?
why: Both are C₄H₁₀O, but the atoms are connected differently.

stem: What is the relationship between cis- and trans-but-2-ene?
why: The atoms are connected in the same order; only the arrangement across the double bond differs.
