stem: A reaction has ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0. Explain how the temperature affects whether it is thermodynamically favorable.
why: Compare ΔH and TΔS.
a: At low temperature the negative ΔH dominates and ΔG < 0; at high temperature the positive −TΔS dominates and ΔG becomes positive.

stem: Calculate the temperature (in K) at which a reaction with ΔH = +60 kJ/mol and ΔS = +0.15 kJ/(mol·K) becomes thermodynamically favorable.
why: ΔG = 0 at the crossover.
a: Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS = 60/0.15 = 400 K. Above 400 K the reaction is favorable.

stem: What does K > 1 say about the equilibrium position?
why: K = [products]/[reactants].
a: The products are favored at equilibrium.

stem: Explain the relationship between the sign of ΔG° and the size of K.
why: Negative ΔG° favors products.
a: If ΔG° < 0, K > 1 (products favored); if ΔG° > 0, K < 1 (reactants favored); if ΔG° = 0, K = 1.

stem: Two reactions have ΔG° = −20 and −5 kJ/mol. Which has the larger K and why?
why: K increases exponentially as ΔG° becomes more negative.
a: The −20 kJ/mol reaction, because a more negative ΔG° corresponds to a larger K.

stem: Define activation energy.
why: Height of the hill.
a: The energy difference between the reactants and the transition state, the barrier the reaction must overcome.

stem: Explain why a reaction can be thermodynamically favorable but extremely slow.
why: Thermodynamics vs kinetics.
a: ΔG tells where equilibrium lies, but the rate depends on Eₐ; a high barrier makes the reaction slow even if ΔG is negative.

stem: Explain why raising the temperature increases the rate of a reaction.
why: Energy distribution.
a: More molecules have kinetic energy above Eₐ, so more collisions are productive.

stem: Rate = k[A][B] for a one-step reaction. What happens to the rate if [A] is tripled and [B] is halved?
why: Multiply the individual factors.

stem: For a first-order reaction Rate = k[A], what happens to the rate when [A] is tripled?
why: Rate is directly proportional to [A].

stem: On an energy diagram, what do the peaks and the valleys represent?
why: Peaks are unstable; valleys are short-lived species.
a: Peaks are transition states; valleys are intermediates.

stem: Describe the energy diagram of a one-step, exergonic reaction.
why: Start high, end low, one hump.
a: The products are at lower energy than the reactants with a single peak (the transition state) between them.

stem: Describe the energy diagram of an endergonic reaction.
why: End higher than start.
a: The products are at higher free energy than the reactants, with the transition state higher than both.

stem: A two-step reaction has transition states at 80 and 60 kJ/mol above the reactants and an intermediate at 30 kJ/mol. Which step is rate-determining, and what is its activation energy?
why: The highest barrier from the preceding valley or start.
a: The first step, because its transition state is highest; its activation energy is 80 kJ/mol.

stem: Why is the intermediate in a two-step reaction not an isolable product in most cases?
why: Short-lived.
a: It sits in a shallow energy valley and has a small barrier to the next step, so it reacts quickly.

stem: Define nucleophile and electrophile.
why: Nucleus-loving vs electron-loving.
a: A nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a bond; an electrophile accepts an electron pair.

stem: Identify the nucleophile and the electrophile in the reaction shown.
why: Follow the arrow from donor to acceptor.
a: The hydroxide ion is the nucleophile (lone pair donor); the carbocation is the electrophile (positive, electron-poor).

stem: Which is the better nucleophile, HO⁻ or H₂O? Explain.
why: Charged species are usually better nucleophiles.
a: HO⁻, because the negative charge makes its lone pairs more available to donate.

stem: Can a species act as both a nucleophile and a base? Explain the difference in what they attack.
why: Same electron pair, different target.
a: Yes. A base uses its electrons to take a proton (attack H); a nucleophile uses them to attack an electron-poor atom, usually carbon.

stem: List the four patterns of arrow pushing.
why: Klein section 6.8.
a: Nucleophilic attack, loss of a leaving group, proton transfer and carbocation rearrangement.

stem: Which arrow-pushing pattern is shown? Draw the product.
why: The bond breaks and the electrons go to the more electronegative atom.
a: Loss of a leaving group: the C-Br bond electrons move to bromine, giving a tertiary carbocation and Br⁻.

stem: Draw the curved arrow(s) for hydroxide attacking the carbocation and draw the product.
why: The lone pair forms the new bond.
a: One arrow from a lone pair on HO⁻ to the positively charged carbon, giving (CH₃)₃COH.

stem: Describe how nucleophilic attack and loss of a leaving group are related to each other, using the SN1 mechanism as an example.
why: SN1 is a two-step process.
a: In SN1, the leaving group departs first, creating a carbocation, and then the nucleophile attacks the cation; they are separate steps.

stem: Why does protonating an alcohol allow it to undergo substitution?
why: Better leaving group.
a: It converts the poor leaving group HO⁻ into water, a good leaving group.

stem: Describe the steps of an acid-catalyzed substitution of an alcohol by bromide through a carbocation intermediate.
why: Protonate, leave, attack.
a: Proton transfer to the OH, loss of water to form the carbocation, then nucleophilic attack by Br⁻ on the carbocation.

stem: Why do arrow-pushing steps in a mechanism usually combine two patterns in one step (for example, E2)?
why: E2 is concerted.
a: The base attacks the proton while the leaving group departs; several curved arrows move electrons simultaneously in a single step.

stem: State two rules for drawing curved arrows.
why: Arrows show electron movement.
a: The arrow starts at a lone pair or bond (the electron source) and points to an atom or bond that will receive them; never start from a positive charge or an atom.

stem: A student draws a curved arrow starting at a carbocation. What is wrong?
why: The tail needs electrons.
a: Curved arrows must start at electrons (a lone pair or bond). A positive charge has no electrons to move.

stem: Show the curved arrow(s) for loss of the leaving group in the substrate shown.
why: The bond electrons leave with the halogen.
a: Draw one arrow from the C-Br bond to bromine, producing a carbocation and Br⁻.

stem: Draw the curved arrow for the methyl shift that converts the secondary carbocation shown into a tertiary carbocation.
why: The bond pair moves toward the cation.
a: One arrow from the C-CH₃ bond to the carbon bearing the positive charge.

stem: Why do carbocations rearrange?
why: Greater stability.
a: To form a more stable carbocation (primary → secondary → tertiary).

stem: Rank the carbocations methyl, primary, secondary and tertiary by stability.
why: More alkyl groups = more stable.

stem: Explain what is moving in a hydride shift and where it goes.
why: H⁻ moves with two electrons.
a: A hydrogen with its bonding pair of electrons moves from a carbon to the adjacent carbocation.

stem: A secondary carbocation is adjacent to a tertiary carbon bearing one hydrogen. Draw the possible rearrangement and name the product cation type.
why: Move H with its electrons.
a: A hydride shifts from the tertiary carbon to the cationic carbon, producing a tertiary carbocation.

stem: Explain why a primary carbocation adjacent to a quaternary carbon will rearrange by a methyl shift, but one adjacent to a CH₂ group with no branching will not give a more stable cation.
why: Compare the cation types formed.
a: A methyl shift from the quaternary carbon makes a tertiary cation; with unbranched neighbours a hydride shift only produces a secondary cation, which is still an improvement but less dramatic.

stem: Sketch in words an energy diagram for a two-step SN1 reaction, naming the intermediate and the rate-determining step.
why: The first step has the larger barrier.
a: Reactants rise to the first transition state (loss of the leaving group, rate-determining), fall into the carbocation intermediate valley, rise to a smaller second peak (nucleophilic attack) and fall to products.

stem: A reaction has ΔG° = +15 kJ/mol. Are reactants or products favored at equilibrium?
why: Positive ΔG° gives K < 1.
a: Reactants are favored, because K < 1 when ΔG° is positive.

stem: Classify each as a nucleophile or an electrophile: NH₃, (CH₃)₃C⁺, Br⁻, H₃O⁺.
why: Look for lone pairs versus electron deficiency.
a: NH₃ and Br⁻ are nucleophiles (lone pairs); (CH₃)₃C⁺ and H₃O⁺ are electrophiles (electron poor).

stem: Which has the higher rate: a reaction with Eₐ = 40 kJ/mol or one with Eₐ = 80 kJ/mol at the same temperature? Explain.
why: Lower barrier, faster rate.
a: The 40 kJ/mol reaction, because more molecules have enough energy to cross the smaller barrier.

stem: In a substitution reaction, what happens?
why: Substitution swaps one group for another; elimination forms a π bond.

o.v: A π bond is formed and a leaving group is lost
Two molecules add across a double bond
A leaving group is replaced by another group

stem: In an elimination reaction of an alkyl halide, what is formed?
why: The halide and a β hydrogen are lost to form a C=C bond.

stem: Which is a good leaving group?
why: Good leaving groups are weak bases that are stable on their own.

stem: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂Br?
why: The halogen is a substituent on the three-carbon chain, numbered from the end nearest it.

stem: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
why: Number from the end nearest the chlorine.

stem: What is the IUPAC name of the compound shown?
why: The longest chain has five carbons; the lowest locants are 2 and 4, with the bromo group named first alphabetically.

stem: Classify the alkyl halide 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
why: The carbon bearing the bromine is bonded to three other carbons.

stem: Classify the alkyl halide shown.
why: The carbon bearing the halogen is attached to only one other carbon.

stem: What does SN2 stand for?
why: The rate depends on two species.

stem: The SN2 mechanism proceeds:
why: Bond formation and bond breaking occur at the same time.

o.v: In two steps through a carbocation

stem: From which direction does the nucleophile attack in an SN2 reaction?
why: The nucleophile attacks the σ* orbital opposite the leaving group.

o.v: From the side opposite the leaving group (back-side attack)
From the same side as the leaving group
In the plane of the molecule

stem: What is the stereochemical outcome of an SN2 reaction at a chirality center?
why: The three other groups flip like an umbrella in the wind.

stem: Which substrate reacts fastest by SN2?
why: Less steric hindrance means faster SN2.

stem: Rank the alkyl bromides from fastest to slowest SN2: 1° , 2°, 3°, methyl.
why: Steric hindrance slows the back-side attack.

stem: The (S)-2-bromobutane shown reacts with NaOH in an SN2 reaction. What is the configuration of the butan-2-ol formed?
why: SN2 inverts the configuration; here the priority order is unchanged so the label flips.

stem: In the SN2 reaction of 1-bromobutane with NaCN, what is the product?
why: Cyanide replaces bromine, adding one carbon.

stem: Which factor does NOT speed up an SN2 reaction?
why: More substituents block the back-side attack.

o.v: Making the substrate more substituted at the reacting carbon

stem: Which is the stronger nucleophile in a polar protic solvent: I⁻ or F⁻?
why: In protic solvents the small anion is held tightly by hydrogen bonds; the larger iodide is more polarizable.

stem: Which is the stronger nucleophile: CH₃O⁻ or CH₃OH?
why: A negatively charged species is generally a stronger nucleophile than its neutral conjugate acid.

stem: Which reagent is both a strong nucleophile and a weak base?
why: Iodide is polarizable and the conjugate base of a strong acid.

stem: Which reagent is a strong base but a poor nucleophile because of its size?
why: The bulky tert-butoxide cannot easily attack carbon but can remove a proton.

stem: What does E2 stand for?
why: The rate depends on both the substrate and the base.

stem: In an E2 reaction, which pattern of arrows applies?
why: The base removes a β hydrogen as the leaving group leaves.

o.v: Loss of a leaving group only
Proton transfer and loss of the leaving group at the same time

stem: In E2, the β hydrogen and the leaving group must be:
why: Anti-coplanar alignment allows the orbitals to overlap in the transition state.

stem: What is the major organic product of 2-bromopropane with sodium ethoxide in ethanol (heat)?
why: A strong base with a secondary halide favors E2.

stem: Which alkene is most stable?
why: Hyperconjugation stabilises substituted alkenes.

stem: Which is the most stable alkene?
why: The trisubstituted alkene is more stable than the di- or monosubstituted ones.

stem: Which is more stable: cis- or trans-but-2-ene, and why?
why: Steric strain destabilizes the cis isomer.

o.v: trans, because the methyl groups are farther apart and there is less steric strain
cis, because the dipole is larger

stem: Which cycloalkene is least able to contain a trans double bond?
why: A trans double bond in a small ring would be too strained.

stem: In an E2 reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane with sodium ethoxide, the major product is:
why: The Zaitsev (more substituted) alkene is favored with a small base.

stem: Using potassium tert-butoxide instead of ethoxide on 2-bromo-2-methylbutane gives mostly:
why: A bulky base removes the less hindered β proton, giving the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene.

stem: An E2 reaction produces a new stereogenic alkene. Which isomer is typically major?
why: The more stable alkene forms faster.

stem: Which β hydrogens of a cyclohexyl bromide can undergo E2 elimination?
why: In a chair, the leaving group and the hydrogen must both be axial.

o.v: Only those anti-coplanar to the bromine (axial-axial)
Only hydrogens on the same face as Br

stem: What does SN1 stand for?
why: The slow step involves only the substrate.

stem: In an SN1 reaction, the rate-determining step is:
why: The first step has the highest barrier.

o.v: Loss of the leaving group to give a carbocation

stem: Which substrate reacts fastest by SN1?
why: A tertiary carbocation is the most stable.

stem: A chirality center undergoes SN1 substitution. The product is typically:
why: The planar carbocation can be attacked from either face.

stem: Which species is an intermediate in E1 and SN1 reactions?
why: Both mechanisms start with loss of the leaving group.

stem: A tertiary alkyl halide with a strong base (NaOEt) gives mainly:
why: A strong base with a hindered substrate favors elimination.

stem: A primary alkyl halide with a strong nucleophile that is a weak base (NaCN) gives mainly:
why: Unhindered substrate plus good nucleophile gives SN2.

stem: A tertiary alkyl halide in warm ethanol (no strong base) gives:
why: The solvent is a weak nucleophile and weak base.

o.v: A mixture of SN1 and E1 products

stem: Which conditions favor E2 over SN2 for a secondary alkyl halide?
why: Heat and strong or bulky bases favor elimination.

o.v: A strong, bulky base and heat
A good nucleophile that is a weak base
A polar protic solvent with no base

stem: Which substrate/reagent pair gives mainly the SN2 product?
why: Only the primary halide with a nucleophile that is a weak base gives SN2.

stem: Why is the OH group of an alcohol a poor leaving group?
why: Strong bases are poor leaving groups.

stem: What converts an alcohol into a good leaving group for substitution?
why: Water (after protonation) and TsO⁻ are good leaving groups.

o.v: Treating it with a base only
Protonation with a strong acid or conversion to a tosylate

stem: To convert 1-bromobutane into butan-1-ol with high yield, which reagent is best?
why: A primary halide with a good nucleophile gives SN2.

stem: To make 2-methylbut-1-ene from 2-bromo-2-methylbutane the best reagent is:
why: A bulky base gives the Hofmann product.

stem: Which is a polar protic solvent?
why: Protic solvents have an O-H or N-H group.

stem: SN2 reactions are generally fastest in:
why: Aprotic solvents do not hydrogen-bond to the nucleophile.

stem: Which solvent favors SN1 reactions by stabilizing the carbocation and leaving group?
why: Protic solvents solvate ions through hydrogen bonding and ion-dipole interactions.

stem: In an addition reaction to an alkene, what happens?
why: The π bond breaks and two new σ bonds form.

o.v: Two groups add across the double bond and the π bond is lost
A proton and a leaving group are lost

stem: Which small alkene is the largest-volume starting material of the chemical industry?
why: Ethylene is made by cracking petroleum.

stem: What is the degree of substitution of the double bond in 2-methylbut-2-ene?
why: Three alkyl groups are attached to the double bond carbons.

stem: What is the degree of substitution of the double bond in 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene?
why: Four alkyl groups are attached to the alkene carbons.

stem: What is the IUPAC name of the alkene shown?
why: Number to give the double bond the lowest locant, then name the substituent.

stem: Why are addition reactions disfavored at high temperature?
why: Two molecules become one, so entropy decreases.

o.v: ΔS is negative, so −TΔS opposes the reaction at high T

stem: What is the major product of the reaction of propene with HBr?
why: Markovnikov addition puts Br on the more substituted carbon.

stem: Markovnikov addition of HX puts the halogen on:
why: The more stable carbocation forms first.

o.v: A carbon next to the double bond
The more substituted carbon of the double bond

stem: What is the intermediate in the addition of HBr to an alkene?
why: Protonation of the alkene gives a carbocation, which Br⁻ then attacks.

stem: What is the major product when 2-methylpropene reacts with HBr?
why: The tertiary carbocation is the intermediate.

stem: What is the major product when propene reacts with HBr in the presence of peroxides (ROOR)?
why: Peroxides lead to a radical mechanism and anti-Markovnikov addition.

stem: The addition of HBr to 3-methylbut-1-ene gives mainly 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. This is because:
why: A carbocation rearrangement gives the more stable cation.

o.v: A hydride shift converts a secondary carbocation to a tertiary one
HBr adds in an anti-Markovnikov sense

stem: Adding HCl to 1-methylcyclohexene gives a product with how many stereoisomers?
why: The tertiary chloride is achiral because the ring is symmetric.

o.v: One (the product has no chirality center)

stem: Hydrohalogenation of but-1-ene gives 2-bromobutane. What is the stereochemical result?
why: The planar carbocation is attacked from either face.

stem: What is the major product when 2-methylpropene is treated with H₂O and H₂SO₄?
why: Markovnikov hydration gives the tertiary alcohol.

stem: Which reaction conditions give an alkene from an alcohol?
why: Concentrated acid favors elimination; dilute acid favors hydration.

stem: Why is acid-catalyzed hydration of 3-methylbut-1-ene a poor way to make 3-methylbutan-2-ol?
why: The secondary cation rearranges to a tertiary cation.

o.v: A carbocation rearrangement gives a different alcohol

stem: Oxymercuration-demercuration is the addition of:
why: The mercurinium ion prevents rearrangement.

o.v: H and Br across a double bond
Two OH groups to the same face
H and OH across a double bond without carbocation rearrangements

stem: What is the product of 3-methylbut-1-ene with (1) Hg(OAc)₂, H₂O; (2) NaBH₄?
why: Markovnikov hydration without rearrangement gives the secondary alcohol.

stem: What is the major product of propene with (1) BH₃·THF; (2) H₂O₂, NaOH?
why: Hydroboration-oxidation gives anti-Markovnikov hydration.

stem: Hydroboration-oxidation proceeds with which stereochemistry?
why: H and B add to the same face in a concerted step.

o.v: Anti addition of H and OH
Syn addition of H and OH

stem: Hydroboration-oxidation of 1-methylcyclohexene gives which product?
why: OH goes to the less substituted carbon and syn addition of H and OH places H and OH on the same face, leaving CH₃ and OH trans.

stem: Which statement about BH₃ addition is correct?
why: The addition is concerted with boron on the less substituted carbon.

o.v: Boron attaches to the less hindered carbon and H adds to the more substituted carbon
Boron attaches to the more substituted carbon

stem: Which reagents hydrogenate an alkene?
why: A metal catalyst is required.

o.v: H₂ with Pt, Pd or Ni

stem: Catalytic hydrogenation proceeds with:
why: Both H atoms are delivered from the catalyst surface to the same face.

stem: Which product is formed when 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene is hydrogenated with H₂, Pt?
why: Syn addition of H₂ puts both methyl groups on the same face.

stem: A homogeneous catalyst is one that:
why: Homogeneous means the same phase as the reactants.

o.v: Is a solid not soluble in the solvent
Is soluble in the reaction mixture

stem: What is the intermediate in the bromination of an alkene with Br₂?
why: A bridged three-membered ring forms.

stem: What is the product of cyclohexene with Br₂ in CH₂Cl₂?
why: The bromonium ion is opened from the opposite face, so the addition is anti.

stem: The addition of Br₂ to an alkene is:
why: The bromide attacks the bromonium ion from the side opposite the Br bridge.

stem: When Br₂ is added to an alkene in water, where does OH end up?
why: The more substituted carbon of the bromonium ion carries more positive charge.

stem: What is the product of Br₂ and H₂O with propene?
why: OH adds to the more substituted carbon; Br adds to the terminal carbon.

stem: What is the product of cyclohexene with (1) mCPBA; (2) H₃O⁺?
why: Epoxidation followed by acid-catalyzed opening gives anti dihydroxylation.

stem: What is the product of cyclohexene with OsO₄ then NaHSO₃/H₂O?
why: OsO₄ adds both oxygens to the same face: syn dihydroxylation.

stem: Which reagent can convert an alkene to a syn diol?
why: OsO₄ (or cold, dilute KMnO₄) gives syn dihydroxylation.

stem: What is formed first from an alkene and mCPBA?
why: The peroxy acid transfers an oxygen atom to the alkene.

stem: Ozonolysis of an alkene followed by DMS cleaves the double bond to give:
why: Each alkene carbon becomes a C=O.

stem: Which compounds form from 2-methylbut-2-ene with (1) O₃; (2) DMS?
why: Cleavage of the double bond gives acetaldehyde and acetone.

stem: Ozonolysis of cyclohexene (O₃ then DMS) gives:
why: The ring is opened to a dialdehyde.

stem: Which alkene gives a single product (propanal) when treated with O₃ then DMS?
why: A symmetrical alkene gives two identical carbonyl compounds.

stem: Which reagent adds H and OH to an alkene with anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry?
why: Hydroboration-oxidation gives the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.

stem: Which of these does NOT proceed through a carbocation intermediate?
why: Hydroboration is concerted.

stem: What three questions help you predict an addition product?
why: These are the questions listed in Klein section 8.14.

o.v: Number of carbons, rings and π bonds
Which groups add, regiochemistry and stereochemistry

stem: What sequence converts 1-bromopropane into 2-bromopropane?
why: Eliminate to propene, then add HBr in a Markovnikov sense.

stem: To convert cyclohexene into cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol, use:
why: Syn dihydroxylation.

stem: To convert 1-methylcyclohexene to 2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (trans), use:
why: Anti-Markovnikov hydration (syn addition).

stem: To convert 2-bromo-2-methylpropane into 2-methylpropan-1-ol, a good route is:
why: Eliminate to the alkene, then add water anti-Markovnikov.

stem: How many carbon atoms are in the longest chain containing the double bond of 2-methylbut-2-ene?
why: But- means four carbons; the methyl is a substituent.

stem: In the addition of HBr to an alkene, which species acts as the electrophile in the first step?
why: The π bond attacks the proton of HBr.

stem: What is the product of 2-methylpropene with H₂, Pt?
why: Hydrogenation converts C=C to C-C.

stem: Define an addition reaction and give an example.
why: The π bond is converted into two σ bonds.
a: Two groups add across a double bond; for example CH₂=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br.

stem: What kind of bond is broken and what is formed in an addition to an alkene?
why: π to two σ.
a: The π bond is broken and two new σ bonds are formed.

stem: Name two alkenes produced industrially by cracking petroleum.
why: Smallest alkenes.

stem: Classify the double bond of 2-methylbut-2-ene as mono-, di-, tri- or tetrasubstituted.
why: Count the alkyl groups on the double bond.
a: Trisubstituted: three alkyl groups are on the double bond carbons.

stem: Draw 3-methylcyclohexene.
why: The double bond gets locants 1 and 2.
a: A six-membered ring with a double bond between C1 and C2 and a methyl group on C3.

stem: Name the compound shown, giving its E/Z descriptor.
why: Rank the groups on each alkene carbon.

stem: Explain why alkene hydrogenation is thermodynamically favorable at room temperature.
why: Bond energies.
a: A weak π bond and an H-H bond are converted into two stronger C-H σ bonds, so ΔH is strongly negative.

stem: Explain why elimination becomes more favorable relative to addition as temperature increases.
why: Entropy.
a: Elimination increases the number of molecules (ΔS > 0), so the −TΔS term makes ΔG more negative at high temperature.

stem: Draw the major product of 2-methylbut-2-ene with HCl.
why: Markovnikov.

stem: Draw the major product of propene with HBr in the presence of peroxides and state the regiochemistry.
why: Peroxides change the mechanism.

stem: Explain why HBr adds to propene to give 2-bromopropane rather than 1-bromopropane.
why: Stability of the intermediate decides.
a: Protonation at the terminal carbon gives a secondary carbocation, more stable than the primary cation from the other orientation; Br⁻ then attacks the secondary carbocation.

stem: Show the first step of the mechanism of HBr with propene using curved arrows.
why: Two arrows.
a: One arrow from the π bond to the H of HBr and one from the H-Br bond to Br, giving a secondary carbocation and Br⁻.

stem: Predict the product of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene with HCl and explain why it is not the direct Markovnikov product.
why: Look for a rearrangement.
a: 2-Chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane: the secondary carbocation rearranges by a methyl shift to a tertiary carbocation before chloride attacks.

stem: When HBr adds to but-1-ene, how many stereoisomers are formed, and in what ratio?
why: Planar intermediate.
a: Two: the R and S enantiomers of 2-bromobutane in a 1:1 (racemic) ratio, because the planar carbocation is attacked equally from both faces.

stem: What reagents add water to an alkene with Markovnikov regiochemistry?
why: Aqueous acid.
a: H₂O with H₂SO₄ or H₃O⁺ (acid-catalyzed hydration).

stem: Draw the product of 1-methylcyclohexene with H₂O, H₂SO₄.
why: Markovnikov: OH on the more substituted carbon.

stem: Describe the three steps of the mechanism of acid-catalyzed hydration of propene.
why: Protonate, attack, deprotonate.
a: 1) Protonation of the alkene gives a secondary carbocation. 2) Water attacks the carbocation, giving an oxonium ion. 3) Deprotonation by water gives propan-2-ol.

stem: How do you favor the alkene when converting an alcohol to an alkene and the alcohol when hydrating an alkene?
why: Le Chatelier.
a: Use concentrated acid and heat to favor the alkene; dilute acid (excess water) to favor the alcohol.

stem: What advantage does oxymercuration-demercuration have over acid-catalyzed hydration?
why: The mercurinium ion.
a: It does not involve a free carbocation, so no rearrangement occurs.

stem: Draw the product of 3-methylbut-1-ene with (1) Hg(OAc)₂, H₂O; (2) NaBH₄.
why: No carbocation rearrangement.

stem: What reagents add H and OH to an alkene with anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry?
why: Hydroboration-oxidation.

stem: Draw the product of 2-methylpropene with (1) BH₃·THF; (2) H₂O₂, NaOH.
why: OH goes to the less substituted carbon.

stem: Explain the stereochemical outcome of hydroboration-oxidation of 1-methylcyclohexene.
why: Syn addition of H and B.
a: H and OH add to the same face (syn), so the product is trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol (CH₃ and OH trans), formed as a racemate.

stem: Why is no carbocation rearrangement observed in hydroboration?
why: One step, no cation.
a: The reaction is concerted: no carbocation is formed, so there is nothing to rearrange.

stem: What reagents are needed to hydrogenate an alkene?
why: Heterogeneous catalysts.
a: H₂ and a metal catalyst (Pd, Pt or Ni).

stem: To convert 2-methylbutane into 2-methylbut-2-ene, a good route is:
why: Selective radical bromination, then E2 elimination.

stem: To convert propane into propene, which two steps are best?
why: Brominate (mostly at C2), then eliminate with a strong base.

stem: What is a radical, and what arrow shows its reactions?
why: One electron per arrow.
a: A radical has an unpaired electron; its reactions are drawn with fishhook (single-headed) arrows.

stem: Rank the radicals methyl, primary, secondary and tertiary by stability.
why: More alkyl groups stabilise the radical.

stem: Explain why the allyl radical is more stable than a primary alkyl radical.
why: Draw both resonance structures.
a: The unpaired electron is delocalised over two carbons through resonance.

stem: Draw the two resonance structures of the allyl radical.
why: Move one electron with fishhook arrows.
a: CH₂=CH-CH₂• ↔ •CH₂-CH=CH₂; the radical is shared by the two terminal carbons.

stem: Why is a vinylic radical not stabilised by resonance?
why: Consider orbital alignment.
a: The unpaired electron is in an sp² orbital in the plane of the molecule, perpendicular to the π system, so it cannot overlap with the π bond.

stem: Name the three stages of a radical chain mechanism.
why: Start, continue, end.

stem: List the six kinds of radical steps.
why: Klein section 10.2.
a: Homolytic cleavage, addition to a π bond, hydrogen abstraction, halogen abstraction, elimination and coupling.

stem: Classify Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃• as initiation, propagation or termination, and as a step type.
why: One radical consumed, one produced.

stem: Explain why a termination step ends the chain.
why: Radicals are consumed.
a: Two radicals combine into a stable molecule, so no radical is left to continue the cycle.

stem: Write the initiation step of the chlorination of methane.
why: Weakest bond.
a: Cl-Cl → 2 Cl• (homolytic cleavage by light or heat).

stem: Write both propagation steps of the chlorination of methane.
why: Hydrogen abstraction then halogen abstraction.
a: Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + CH₃•; CH₃• + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•.

stem: Show that the two propagation steps add up to the net reaction.
why: Add and cancel the radicals.
a: Cl• + CH₄ + CH₃• + Cl₂ → HCl + CH₃• + CH₃Cl + Cl•; cancelling Cl• and CH₃• leaves CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl.

stem: Give three possible termination steps in the chlorination of methane.
why: Two radicals combine.
a: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; CH₃• + Cl• → CH₃Cl; CH₃• + CH₃• → CH₃CH₃.

stem: Why is a small amount of light enough to convert a large amount of methane to chloromethane?
why: Chain reaction.
a: The propagation steps form a chain reaction in which each chlorine radical regenerates itself and can cause many cycles.

stem: Use C-H 414, Cl-Cl 243, C-Cl 339 and H-Cl 431 kJ/mol to calculate ΔH for each propagation step of methane chlorination.
why: Bonds broken minus bonds formed.
a: Step 1: 414 − 431 = −17 kJ/mol. Step 2: 243 − 339 = −96 kJ/mol. Overall −113 kJ/mol.

stem: Which is more practical in the laboratory: radical chlorination or radical iodination? Explain briefly.
why: Only Cl and Br are useful.
a: Chlorination, since the iodination propagation step is too unfavorable (only chlorination and bromination are practical).

stem: Explain why radical halogenation occurs more readily at tertiary hydrogens.
why: Radical stability.
a: Abstracting a tertiary hydrogen forms the most stable (tertiary) radical, with the lowest energy transition state.

stem: Which is more selective, bromination or chlorination, and why?
why: Late transition state.
a: Bromination; its hydrogen abstraction step is endothermic with a late transition state, which resembles the radical and magnifies stability differences.

stem: Draw the major product of isobutane with Br₂, hν and explain.
why: Selectivity of Br•.
a: 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane; bromine is highly selective for the tertiary hydrogen.

stem: Draw all monochlorination products of propane.
why: Two types of hydrogen.

stem: Chlorination of 2-methylbutane gives four monochloro constitutional isomers. Draw them.
why: Count the types of hydrogens.

stem: Radical bromination of butane at C2 creates a chirality center. What is the stereochemical result?
why: Planar radical.
a: A racemic mixture of (R)- and (S)-2-bromobutane, because the radical is planar and Br₂ attacks either face.

stem: Explain why bromination of optically pure (R)-3-methylhexane at C3 gives an optically inactive product.
why: Radical intermediate.
a: The radical at C3 is planar and achiral, and Br₂ attacks either face equally, giving a racemic mixture.

stem: Why does the chirality of a starting material not control the outcome of a radical substitution at that center?
why: Planar radical.
a: Because the intermediate radical is planar, so the original configuration is lost.

stem: What reagent is used for allylic bromination?
why: NBS.
a: N-Bromosuccinimide (NBS) with light or a radical initiator.

stem: Draw the product of cyclohexene with NBS, hν.
why: Allylic position.

stem: Draw the product of propene with NBS, hν.
why: Allylic bromination.

stem: Why does Br₂ at high concentration add to alkenes but NBS gives allylic substitution?
why: Concentration of Br₂.
a: NBS keeps the concentration of Br₂ very low, so the ionic addition via a bromonium ion is slow compared with the radical chain substitution.

stem: Explain why allylic bromination of 1-butene can give two products.
why: Two resonance structures.
a: The allylic radical is resonance-stabilised, so Br₂ can attack either end, giving 3-bromobut-1-ene and 1-bromobut-2-ene.

stem: Outline the mechanism of allylic bromination of cyclohexene with NBS: name the two propagation steps.
why: Hydrogen abstraction then halogen abstraction.
a: Br• abstracts an allylic hydrogen to give a resonance-stabilised allylic radical and HBr; the radical abstracts a Br from Br₂ to give 3-bromocyclohexene and Br•.

stem: What are CFCs, and what problem did they cause?
why: Ozone depletion.
a: Chlorofluorocarbons; they release chlorine radicals in the stratosphere that destroy the ozone layer.

stem: Why were HFCs introduced as replacements for CFCs?
why: No chlorine.
a: HFCs contain no chlorine, so they do not generate chlorine radicals that destroy ozone.

stem: What is autooxidation?
why: Oxidation by O₂ in air.
a: A radical chain reaction of organic compounds with atmospheric oxygen that forms hydroperoxides.

stem: Explain how BHT preserves foods.
why: Radical trap.
a: BHT is a radical scavenger: it donates a hydrogen atom to peroxy radicals, forming a stable radical that does not continue the chain.

stem: Name two natural antioxidants.
why: Protect cell membranes.

stem: What conditions cause HBr to add to an alkene in an anti-Markovnikov sense?
why: Radical mechanism.

stem: Draw the product of propene with HBr in the presence of peroxides.
why: Anti-Markovnikov.

stem: Explain the regiochemistry of radical addition of HBr to propene.
why: More stable radical.
a: Br• adds to the terminal carbon, forming the more stable secondary radical; this radical then abstracts H from HBr, giving 1-bromopropane.

stem: Why does radical addition work for HBr but not for HCl or HI?
why: One of the propagation steps is unfavorable.
a: For HCl the hydrogen abstraction step is too endothermic; for HI the addition of I• to the alkene is too unfavorable.

stem: What monomer gives polyvinyl chloride (PVC)?
why: CH₂=CHCl.

stem: Explain why polymerisation of ethylene through a radical process gives chain branching.
why: Hydrogen abstraction.
a: A growing chain radical can abstract a hydrogen from within its own chain (backbiting), creating a new radical site from which a branch grows.

stem: Draw the repeating unit of polyvinyl chloride and the monomer it comes from.
why: The π bond opens.

stem: What is cracking?
why: Radical process.
a: Breaking larger hydrocarbons into smaller ones, such as gasoline-range alkanes and alkenes, at high temperature.

stem: Propose a synthesis of 2-methylbut-2-ene from 2-methylbutane.
why: Brominate, then eliminate.
a: (1) Br₂, hν (selective at the tertiary C-H) to give 2-bromo-2-methylbutane; (2) NaOEt, heat (E2).

stem: Propose a synthesis of trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol from cyclohexane.
why: Radical bromination, elimination, anti dihydroxylation.
a: (1) Br₂, hν; (2) NaOEt, heat to give cyclohexene; (3) mCPBA; (4) H₃O⁺.

stem: Propose a synthesis of 1-bromopropane from propane.
why: Anti-Markovnikov radical addition.
a: (1) Br₂, hν gives mostly 2-bromopropane; (2) NaOEt, heat gives propene; (3) HBr, ROOR gives 1-bromopropane.

stem: Why is radical bromination preferred over chlorination when a single product is wanted?
why: Selectivity.
a: Bromine is much more selective, so it reacts mostly at the most substituted (tertiary) C-H and gives one major product.

stem: Which is more stable, a secondary radical or a primary radical? Give the reason.
why: More alkyl groups, more stable.
a: The secondary radical; its extra alkyl group stabilises the unpaired electron by hyperconjugation, the same trend seen for carbocations.

stem: What does hν mean in a reaction scheme?
why: Light as the initiator.
a: Light (a photon of energy hν) used to start the reaction, here by breaking a weak bond homolytically.

stem: What is a radical inhibitor? Give one example.
why: Radical scavenger.
a: A compound that stops a radical chain by reacting with radicals to form stable products; examples include oxygen and hydroquinone.

stem: What is the product of propene with H₂ and Pt?
why: Catalytic hydrogenation converts C=C to C-C.

stem: What is the product of cyclohexene with Br₂?
why: Addition of Br₂ across the π bond gives trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.

stem: What is the product of 2-bromopropane with NaOEt and heat?
why: A strong base with a secondary halide favors E2.

stem: What is the product of 1-bromobutane with NaCN?
why: Cyanide is a good nucleophile and a weak base: SN2.

stem: Which reagents convert an alkene into an alcohol with Markovnikov regiochemistry?
why: Acid-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov.

stem: Which reagent converts a terminal alkyne into a methyl ketone?
why: Hydration of an alkyne gives a ketone through an enol.

stem: Which reagent converts an alkene into an epoxide?
why: A peroxy acid transfers an oxygen to the alkene.

stem: How can the position of a halogen be changed?
why: Eliminate HX to form an alkene, then add HX in the other orientation.

stem: How can the position of a π bond be changed?
why: Add HX across the alkene, then eliminate in the other direction.

stem: Which sequence converts 1-bromopropane into 2-bromopropane?
why: Eliminate to propene, then add HBr in a Markovnikov sense.

stem: Which sequence converts 1-pentene into 2-pentene?
why: Add HBr to give 2-bromopentane, then eliminate toward the more substituted alkene.

stem: Which sequence converts an alkane into an alkene?
why: Radical bromination, then E2 elimination.

stem: Which sequence converts but-1-ene into but-1-yne?
why: Bromination, double elimination, then protonation.

stem: Which sequence converts an alkyne into a trans alkene?
why: Dissolving-metal reduction.

stem: Which sequence converts cyclohexane into trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol?
why: Halogenate, eliminate, then anti dihydroxylation through the epoxide.

stem: If the carbon skeleton gets larger, which kind of reaction is needed?
why: New carbons must be attached.

stem: If the carbon skeleton gets smaller, which kind of reaction is needed?
why: Ozonolysis splits C=C or C≡C bonds.

o.v: A C-C bond cleavage such as ozonolysis

stem: Which reaction forms a new C-C bond?
why: Alkylation of alkynides is the Klein C-C bond-forming reaction in these chapters.

o.v: An alkynide reacting with a primary alkyl halide

stem: What is the product of propyne with (1) NaNH₂; (2) CH₃CH₂Br?
why: Two carbons are added to the alkyne.

stem: Which reagent sequence converts hex-3-yne into propanoic acid?
why: Ozonolysis of an internal alkyne gives two carboxylic acids.

stem: Which sequence converts acetylene into hex-3-yne?
why: Alkylate both terminal hydrogens.

stem: Which compound is made from cyclohexene by (1) O₃; (2) DMS?
why: The ring is cleaved to a dialdehyde.

stem: Which sequence makes pent-2-yne from propyne?
why: Alkylation of the alkynide.

stem: What two questions should be asked first in a synthesis problem?
why: Klein section 11.3 states these two questions.

o.v: What is the yield? What is the cost?
What is the solvent? What is the temperature?
Does the carbon skeleton change? Does the functional group change identity or position?
How many steps? How many reagents?

stem: Comparing a starting material with a product, the product has two more carbon atoms. What is needed?
why: The skeleton must be extended.

stem: Which transformation changes only the location of a functional group?
why: Both compounds have three carbons and a bromine, but the bromine moves.

stem: The synthesis of butanal from but-1-yne requires:
why: The carbonyl must end up at the terminal carbon.

stem: What is a retrosynthetic analysis?
why: The last step is identified first.

o.v: Working forward from the starting material
Working backward from the product to the starting material
Testing the reaction in the lab

stem: In a retrosynthetic analysis of 2-bromopropane from propane, what is the immediate precursor?
why: Propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane.

stem: A retrosynthesis of cis-hex-3-ene from acetylene and ethyl bromide ends with which last step?
why: The cis alkene is made by partial hydrogenation of the alkyne.

stem: A retrosynthesis of 2-methylpropan-1-ol from 2-methylpropene ends with which last step?
why: Anti-Markovnikov hydration.

stem: Which is the best precursor for a final step of anti-dihydroxylation giving trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol?
why: mCPBA then H₃O⁺ on the alkene.

stem: A target is 2,2-dibromopropane. Which is the best immediate precursor?
why: Two equivalents of HBr add to propyne at the same carbon.

stem: What is green chemistry?
why: It aims to reduce waste and hazards.

o.v: Designing reactions that minimize negative impacts on the environment

stem: What does a high atom economy mean?
why: Less waste is produced.

o.v: The reaction gives high yield only
Most atoms of the reactants end up in the desired product

stem: Atom economy of CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CHBrCH₃ is:
why: An addition uses all atoms of both reactants.

stem: Which has the lower atom economy?
why: Eliminations produce a byproduct (salt plus alcohol).

o.v: Elimination of HBr from 2-bromopropane with NaOEt

stem: Which is generally the best approach to a synthesis problem?
why: Efficiency matters.

o.v: Use as many steps as possible

stem: Why is learning the reagents from Chapters 7 to 10 essential for synthesis?
why: Mastery of reactions is the foundation.

o.v: Each synthesis is built from those known reactions

stem: Which is NOT a good strategy when planning a synthesis?
why: You must control where and how groups are added.

stem: Several different routes give the same correct product. How should you choose?
why: Efficiency and selectivity are priorities.

o.v: Choose the one with the most steps
Prefer the route with fewer steps and better selectivity

stem: To convert propene into 1,2-dibromopropane use:
why: Addition of Br₂ across the double bond.

stem: To convert cyclohexene into cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol use:
why: Syn dihydroxylation.

stem: Which sequence converts 2-bromo-2-methylpropane into 2-methylpropan-1-ol?
why: Eliminate, then anti-Markovnikov hydration.

stem: Which reagent converts an alkene into an alkane?
why: Catalytic hydrogenation.

stem: Which reagents cleave an alkene into two carbonyl compounds?
why: Ozonolysis.

stem: Which reagent adds Br across a double bond?
why: Halogenation of an alkene.

stem: Which reagent brominates the allylic position of an alkene?
why: Allylic bromination.

stem: Which reagent converts a vicinal dibromide into an alkyne?
why: Two successive E2 reactions.

stem: Which change requires C-C bond cleavage?
why: The ring is broken open, so the skeleton changes by cleavage.

stem: Give the reagents to convert propene into propane.
why: Catalytic hydrogenation.
a: H₂ with Pt (or Pd or Ni).

stem: Give the reagents to convert cyclohexene into trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
why: Anti addition.

stem: Give the reagents to convert but-2-yne into trans-but-2-ene.
why: Dissolving-metal reduction.

stem: Give the reagents to convert but-2-yne into cis-but-2-ene.
why: Poisoned catalyst.

stem: Give the reagents to convert 1-methylcyclohexene into 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol and into trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol.
why: Regiochemistry controls the choice.
a: H₂O, H₂SO₄ (Markovnikov) for the first; BH₃·THF then H₂O₂, NaOH (anti-Markovnikov, syn addition) for the second.

stem: Give the product of 3-methylbut-1-ene with (1) Hg(OAc)₂, H₂O; (2) NaBH₄, and explain why this reagent is used instead of H₂SO₄/H₂O.
why: No free carbocation.

stem: Propose a synthesis of 2-bromopropane from 1-bromopropane.
why: Eliminate, then add.

stem: Show how to convert 2-bromopropane into 1-bromopropane in two steps.
why: Radical addition.

stem: Propose a synthesis of pent-2-ene from pent-1-ene.
why: Add then eliminate.
a: (1) HBr (Markovnikov, gives 2-bromopentane); (2) NaOEt, heat (E2, Zaitsev product).

stem: Propose a synthesis of cyclohexene from cyclohexane.
why: Radical bromination then E2.

stem: Propose a synthesis of 3-bromocyclohexene from cyclohexane.
why: Make the alkene, then brominate the allylic position.
a: (1) Br₂, hν; (2) NaOEt, heat to give cyclohexene; (3) NBS, hν (allylic bromination).

stem: Give a three-step route from but-1-ene to but-1-yne.
why: Bromination, then double elimination.

stem: Propose a synthesis of propane-1,2-diol (cis addition irrelevant) from 2-bromopropane.
why: Eliminate, then dihydroxylate.
a: (1) NaOEt, heat to propene; (2) OsO₄, then NaHSO₃ (or mCPBA, then H₃O⁺).

stem: Propose a synthesis of trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol from cyclohexanol.
why: Alkene first, then anti dihydroxylation.
a: (1) H₂SO₄, heat (dehydration) to cyclohexene; (2) mCPBA; (3) H₃O⁺.

stem: Propose a synthesis of 2-methylpropan-1-ol from 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
why: Eliminate then anti-Markovnikov hydration.
a: (1) t-BuOK, heat (E2, gives 2-methylpropene); (2) BH₃·THF; (3) H₂O₂, NaOH.

stem: Propose a synthesis of butanal from but-1-yne.
why: Anti-Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne.
a: (1) Sia₂BH (or 9-BBN); (2) H₂O₂, NaOH; the enol tautomerizes to butanal.

stem: How do you decide whether a synthesis needs C-C bond formation or cleavage?
why: Count the carbons.
a: Compare the number of carbons in the starting material and the product: more carbons needs bond formation, fewer needs bond cleavage.

stem: Propose a synthesis of pent-2-yne from propyne.
why: Alkylate the alkynide.

stem: Propose a synthesis of hex-3-yne from acetylene.
why: Two alkylations.

stem: Propose a synthesis of acetic acid from but-2-yne.
why: Cleavage of the triple bond.
a: (1) O₃; (2) H₂O. Two equivalents of acetic acid form.

stem: Propose a synthesis of acetone from 2-methylbut-2-ene.
why: Ozonolysis.
a: (1) O₃; (2) DMS (the other product is acetaldehyde).

stem: Propose a synthesis of hexanedial from cyclohexene.
why: Cleaves the ring.

stem: Propose a synthesis of cis-pent-2-ene from propyne and bromoethane.
why: Alkylate, then reduce to cis.

stem: Propose a synthesis of trans-hex-3-ene from acetylene and bromoethane.
why: Build hex-3-yne, then dissolving-metal reduction.
a: (1) NaNH₂; (2) CH₃CH₂Br; (3) NaNH₂; (4) CH₃CH₂Br; (5) Na, NH₃(l).

stem: Propose a synthesis of butan-2-one from acetylene and bromoethane.
why: Extend, then hydrate.
a: (1) NaNH₂; (2) CH₃CH₂Br to give but-1-yne; (3) H₂O, H₂SO₄, HgSO₄.

stem: List the two questions to ask when approaching a synthesis problem.
why: Klein 11.3.
a: Is there any change in the carbon skeleton? Is there any change in the identity and/or location of the functional group?

stem: Does converting 1-butene into 1-butyne change the skeleton or only the functional group?
why: Count carbons.
a: Only the functional group; both have four carbons.

stem: Does converting propyne into pent-2-yne change the skeleton? What type of reaction is needed?
why: Compare carbon counts.
a: Yes, it gains two carbons; a C-C bond-forming reaction (alkylation of the alkynide) is needed.

stem: Define retrosynthetic analysis.
why: Backwards.
a: Working backward from the target molecule, identifying the last step first and the preceding compounds in turn until a simple starting material is reached.

stem: Write the retrosynthesis (last two steps) for 1-bromopropane from propane.
why: Work backward.
a: Target ⇒ propene (add HBr, ROOR) ⇒ 2-bromopropane (E2) ⇒ propane (Br₂, hν).

stem: Write the retrosynthesis for trans-cyclohexane-1,2-diol starting from cyclohexane.
why: Last step first.
a: Target ⇐ epoxide/cyclohexene (mCPBA, H₃O⁺) ⇐ bromocyclohexane (NaOEt) ⇐ cyclohexane (Br₂, hν).

stem: Write the retrosynthesis for hex-3-yne from acetylene and bromoethane.
why: Two alkylations.
a: Hex-3-yne ⇐ but-1-yne + ethyl bromide ⇐ acetylene + ethyl bromide, each time via an alkynide.

stem: Write the retrosynthesis for 2,2-dibromopropane from propane.
why: Work back through the alkyne.
a: 2,2-Dibromopropane ⇐ propyne (2 HBr) ⇐ 1,2-dibromopropane (excess NaNH₂) ⇐ propene (Br₂) ⇐ 2-bromopropane (NaOEt) ⇐ propane (Br₂, hν).

stem: Write the retrosynthesis for cis-pent-2-ene starting from acetylene and bromoalkanes.
why: Build the alkyne then reduce.
a: cis-Pent-2-ene ⇐ pent-2-yne (H₂, Lindlar) ⇐ propyne + CH₃CH₂Br (NaNH₂) ⇐ acetylene + CH₃Br (NaNH₂).

stem: Write the retrosynthesis for 2-methylpropan-1-ol starting from 2-methylpropane.
why: Radical bromination is selective for the tertiary C-H.
a: Target ⇐ 2-methylpropene (BH₃; H₂O₂, NaOH) ⇐ 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (t-BuOK or NaOEt) ⇐ 2-methylpropane (Br₂, hν).

stem: Define green chemistry in your own words.
why: Reduce waste and hazard.
a: Designing chemical reactions and processes to minimize their negative effects on the environment.

stem: Calculate the atom economy of CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → CH₃CHBrCH₃.
why: Addition reactions use all atoms.
a: 100%, since all atoms of both reactants appear in the product.

stem: Estimate the atom economy of CH₃CHBrCH₃ + NaOCH₂CH₃ → CH₃CH=CH₂ + NaBr + CH₃CH₂OH. (Molar masses: product 42.1; reactants 123.0 + 68.1.)
why: Product mass divided by total reactant mass.
a: About 22% (42.1/191.1); the rest is wasted as NaBr and ethanol.

stem: Explain why an addition reaction is typically greener than an elimination reaction.
why: Atom economy.
a: Addition incorporates every atom of the reactants in the product (100% atom economy), whereas elimination releases a byproduct such as a salt and an alcohol.

stem: Give two ways a chemist can make a synthesis greener.
why: Many answers are possible.
a: Use fewer steps and reagents, choose safer solvents, use catalysts instead of stoichiometric reagents, or choose routes with higher atom economy.

stem: Why might two correct synthesis routes differ in quality?
why: Efficiency.
a: One may use fewer steps, higher-yielding reactions or more selective reagents; shorter, selective routes are preferred.

stem: Why must regiochemistry be considered when planning an alkene-to-alcohol step?
why: Markovnikov vs anti-Markovnikov.
a: Acid-catalyzed hydration (or oxymercuration) puts OH on the more substituted carbon, hydroboration on the less substituted carbon, so the reagent determines which constitutional isomer forms.

stem: Why does the stereochemistry of an addition step matter in synthesis?
why: Syn vs anti.
a: Syn and anti additions give different stereoisomers (for example, cis vs trans diols), so the reagent must be chosen to give the required stereoisomer.

stem: Propose a synthesis of cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol from bromocyclohexane.
why: Eliminate then syn dihydroxylation.
a: (1) NaOEt, heat (E2) to give cyclohexene; (2) OsO₄, then NaHSO₃/H₂O.

stem: Propose a synthesis of 2-bromopropane from propyne.
why: Reduce the alkyne to the alkene, then add HBr.
a: (1) H₂, Pt (to propane or use Lindlar to propene); (2) with propene, HBr. Using Lindlar: H₂, Lindlar gives propene, then HBr gives 2-bromopropane.

stem: Propose a synthesis of 1,2-dibromocyclohexane from cyclohexane.
why: Make the alkene, then add Br₂.

stem: Propose a synthesis of propanoic acid from hex-3-yne.
why: Cleavage of an internal alkyne.
a: (1) O₃; (2) H₂O (two equivalents of propanoic acid form).

stem: Give the reagents to convert propyne into propene.
why: Partial reduction.

stem: Give the reagents to convert propene into 1,2-dibromopropane.
why: Halogenation.

stem: Give the reagents to convert 2-butene into two molecules of acetaldehyde.
why: Ozonolysis.
